client_context: A 20-year-old star athlete whose performance has been slipping due to partying. Coach gave an ultimatum. Torn between team loyalty and social life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in. Walk-in appointments can feel a little... I don't know, like jumping into cold water. So no agenda from my end — just, whatever brought you here today, we can start there. What's going on for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, um... I mean, my coach kind of — I want to be clear, I chose to come here. He didn't make me. But he said some stuff last week and I guess it just... I don't know, it's been in my head. I don't think I have like a problem or anything. Things have just been a little off lately.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something he said stuck with you, even if you're still figuring out what to do with it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. He said if my split times don't come down before conference, I'm off the relay. And I've been on that team since freshman year, so... it hit different. But I mean — it's not like I'm going out every single night. My teammates party too. Nobody says anything to them.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That relay spot has clearly meant a lot to you. I'm curious — what does it actually mean to you? Like, beyond the event itself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... everything? It's the one thing I've ever been genuinely good at. My whole family drove four hours for my sophomore meet. My dad doesn't really do that stuff. And now I'm just... I'm watching it fall apart and I don't even — I don't know how to stop it. Honestly sometimes I think it's just too late. Like maybe I already blew it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You walked through that door today. That's not nothing — that actually takes a lot.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess... I don't know if just showing up here fixes anything. I just miss how it felt before. Like I used to wake up and actually want to go train. Now I'm exhausted all the time, I feel like garbage at practice, and... I think I've been using the parties to like, not think about any of it. Which is dumb. I know it's dumb.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just... reflect back what I'm hearing, and you tell me if I'm getting it wrong. You've got something that has meant everything — to you, to your family. And somewhere along the way the nights out shifted from blowing off steam to something more like... escape. And now you're here because a part of you, maybe a quiet part, wants something to be different.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that... yeah. Yeah, that's — that's pretty much it. I don't want to be the guy who just threw it all away for nothing, you know? Like I actually think I could turn it around. I just... I don't even know where to start.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You already started.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Maybe I did.

client_context: A 38-year-old mandated by court to attend counseling after a second DUI. Furious about being forced to be here. Sees the system as unfair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I appreciate you coming in. I'm not going to pretend you had a choice about being here — you didn't. I'd rather just be straight with you than waste your time. So what's your take on all this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My take is the judge said show up or lose my license so here I am. Look, maybe this'll be different from the other two times, I don't know. Probably not. But I'm here, so... yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you is wondering if this could actually be different. And part of you has pretty good reasons to doubt that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean — two counselors before this. Both of 'em had the same playbook. 'Do you think your drinking is a problem?' 'Have you considered how this affects others?' And I'm sitting there thinking, okay, what happens if I say no? What happens if I say yes? Either way I feel like I'm walking into a trap and I just... I don't know. It's exhausting, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What made it feel like a trap?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Because they already had their answer. They wanted me to say 'I'm an alcoholic, I'm powerless, my life is unmanageable' — all that. And I'm like, that is not what this is. I work sixty hours a week. I coach my son's baseball team. I pay my bills. Two DUIs doesn't make me some... some skid row guy. I like to drink. I work hard. I deserve to unwind. That's not a disease, that's just — that's my life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You work hard, you show up for your kid, you keep things running — and you've got a clear sense of who you are and who you aren't. That's actually useful to know about yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I do. I'm not — look, I'm not sitting here saying everything's perfect. Okay? I know things aren't perfect. But the way the system treats you, like you're already guilty, like they've already written your story before you even open your mouth... that pisses me off. That's what pisses me off.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And underneath being angry at the system... there's something else you said. That things aren't perfect. I noticed you said it and then moved past it pretty fast.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My wife... she didn't come to court this time. First DUI she was there. Sat right behind me. This time I get a text — 'good luck.' And I don't know, that just... that one hit different. I keep thinking about that text. Three words. She couldn't even — yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you think that text meant? What was she telling you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That she's tired. That's... that's what it means. She's tired. And I get it, I do. I come home most nights and I've already had a few by the time I walk through the door and I'm just — I'm not present, I guess. I'm there but I'm not there. And my kids are getting older and I just... I don't want them to remember me like that. That's not who I want to be. That's really not.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just check if I'm tracking this right. You came in here angry — and that's fair, the situation is what it is. But you're also a guy who coaches his son on weekends, who works sixty hours a week, who noticed something real when his wife sent three words instead of showing up. And you just said something pretty important: this isn't who you want to be. That's not nothing. That's actually a lot.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I... I don't know what doing anything about it even looks like. I've never really — I've always just pushed through things on my own, you know? That's how I was raised. But I'm forty in two years and I don't want to look back at my forties the same way I'm looking at my thirties right now. Does that make sense?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That makes complete sense. And the fact that you're sitting here saying it — not because you have to, but because something in you actually means it — that's the only real starting point there is.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I still think the whole court thing is a racket. I want to be clear about that. But... um... I don't know. Maybe I can actually talk to you. I'm not promising anything. I just — yeah. Maybe.

client_context: A 39-year-old diagnosed with depression who self-medicates with alcohol. Has tried therapy before and dropped out. Skeptical but willing to give it one more try.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in — and I'll skip the whole 'make yourself comfortable, take your time' thing since I hear you're on a clock. I'm Marcus. You must be Derek?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Derek. Look, Dr. Chen basically told me I should come here, so... I'm here. I've got maybe forty minutes before my seminar. Just so you know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Forty minutes is plenty, trust me — I've done a lot with less. So Dr. Chen sent you over. What's your own read on why she thought that was a good idea?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She thinks I drink too much. Which, okay, I drink — but I'm a grad student in my fourth year. That's basically... I mean, that's the culture, right? I don't know. Maybe she's just ticking a box. I had a couple of rough weeks and apparently I mentioned it once and now here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the drinking fits the territory, from where you're standing. Stressful program, everyone does it. And at the same time — rough weeks. That phrase is doing some work. What's been rough?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... I mean, I have depression. Like, diagnosed, I've known that for years. I was in therapy before — couple years back — and I stopped going. It just wasn't... it didn't really help. And lately the depression's been louder and I haven't been sleeping and I'm behind on my dissertation and I just — yeah. Rough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You stopped the therapy before — what happened there? What made it not feel worth continuing?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just felt like we kept going in circles. Like, okay yes, my childhood was hard, I get it, but talking about it every week wasn't getting my work done. And the drinking — I think that's when I started leaning on it more. Like, one drink at night to come down from the day became... more. I don't know. It just kind of crept up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It crept up and you noticed it. That's actually not a small thing — a lot of people are working hard not to notice. You let yourself see it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it's embarrassing more than anything. I'm thirty-nine. I have a master's degree, almost a PhD, and I'm sitting in a college wellness center because I can't feel okay without a drink. And the thing is — it's started happening during the day now. Like, not every day, but... that's new. And I don't love that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: During the day is worth paying attention to — you're already doing that. When it happens, what are you trying to get some relief from? What's the noise you're turning down?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The... the thoughts, I guess. The ones that say you're failing, you're behind, everyone around you knows you're a fraud. The depression stuff. The alcohol just quiets it for a little while. I know it's not a solution. I'm not stupid. I just — I don't know what else works that fast. Nothing else works that fast.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just make sure I'm tracking everything you've shared. You came in because Dr. Chen asked you to, but there's a real part of you that already knows something's shifted. The drinking started as a way to manage the depression — turn down those loud, painful thoughts — and for a while it did the job. But now it's showing up during the day, and that's a line that means something to you. You tried therapy before and it didn't fit, so you've got reason to be skeptical. And you're here anyway.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. That's... yeah. I — my dad had a drinking problem. A real one. I watched it happen. I always said I wouldn't be that guy. And I'm not sure I'm there yet but I can kind of see the road going that direction and it's... that's actually pretty scary to say out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You can see the road. And you don't want to take it. That matters — that's yours, not Dr. Chen's.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. I really don't. And I think — look, I can't just stop drinking if my brain is still on fire. That didn't work the one time I tried. But if we could actually work on the depression piece, like actually, not just talk-about-your-dad stuff... maybe that's something. I don't know. I'm willing to try. Actually try this time.

client_context: A 32-year-old ER nurse who started drinking heavily during the pandemic. Feels guilty but says it's the only way to decompress after traumatic shifts.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know walking into a new place can feel a little strange — especially if you've been through this before and it hasn't quite landed. So I just want to start simple: what's going on for you right now? What brought you in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I, um... I guess I've been drinking more than I should. My boyfriend sat me down last week and I couldn't really argue with what he was saying, and that kind of scared me. Which is — I'm a nurse. An ER nurse. I literally watch what alcohol does to people every single shift. So I know. I'm not here because anyone forced me or anything. I made this appointment myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You see it up close, what it does — and part of you has known for a while. And yet here you are, sitting with that gap between knowing and doing. That's a hard place to live.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. The pandemic kind of... broke something in me, I think. I watched people die alone for two years. You can't just go home and watch TV after that. Wine was the only thing that actually turned my brain off. And now it's just — it's what I do after a shift. It's not like I'm showing up to work drunk or anything. I'm functional. I just need it to decompress.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you imagine your life a year from now — not what it should look like, just what you actually want — what do you see?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I genuinely don't know. I've seen other counselors and I always leave with coping strategies and worksheets and — then a twelve-hour shift happens and someone codes in my bay and a family is screaming in the hallway and the worksheets just... they don't help. Nothing helps. I don't know what's supposed to be different this time. I don't know if anything can be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You keep coming back, even after it hasn't worked. Even when part of you doesn't believe it will. That matters more than you might think.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I have to try, right? Because — okay, the thing is, I've been making mistakes at work. Small ones. But I'm a good nurse. I have always been a good nurse. And lately I've been snapping at residents, missing things I wouldn't have missed before. My charge nurse pulled me aside last month and I just... that got to me. That really got to me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being a good nurse isn't just what you do — it sounds like it's who you are. And right now that feels like it's slipping, and that's terrifying.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. I got into this because I wanted to help people. And now I feel like I'm just... running on fumes. And wine. I can't even remember the last time I felt proud of myself after a shift. Like, actually proud. It used to happen all the time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Is there anything at work recently — even a small moment — that still gave you that feeling? Even a flicker of it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Actually... yeah. Two weeks ago. There was this older man who came in totally alone, terrified before a procedure. And I just — nobody else was going to, so I sat with him for ten minutes and held his hand. When he left he called me an angel. I cried in the bathroom after. But like, the good kind of cry? I don't know. I haven't felt that in a long time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I'm hearing. You came in carrying two years of really serious trauma — people dying, families falling apart, impossible situations. Drinking became a way to survive, and for a while it did exactly that. But now it's starting to cost you something that matters a lot: the kind of nurse you want to be. The one who sits with the scared man. The one who cries the good tears. That person is still here — she just walked through the door.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... yeah. That's it. When you say it like that it doesn't sound as hopeless. Like, I didn't turn into a bad person. I was just trying to survive and now the thing I used to survive is getting in the way of actually living. God. I haven't thought about it like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Given everything you've just said — given the nurse who held that man's hand — what would it mean to you to get more of that back?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It would mean everything. I worked too hard to end up just coasting through shifts half-checked out. I'm tired of feeling like this. I'm not going to sit here and promise you anything — I've learned not to do that. But I'm here. I actually showed up this time, and I think... I think that means something. At least I hope it does.

client_context: A 33-year-old social media influencer whose entire social life revolves around drinking. Multiple friends have expressed concern. Insists it's just her lifestyle.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back. [pause] I know last week left us both sitting with a lot... how are you doing today? Really.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — [exhales] I'm fine. [soft laugh] That's kind of my whole thing, right? Always fine. But yeah, it's been... a lot. The lab results, and then Kayla basically staged an intervention at brunch on Saturday, which was super fun. [flat tone] And my mom called twice. So. I'm here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Kayla. Your mom. The doctor's office. All in the same week. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No, I know, it's just — okay, so the labs. The doctor said my liver enzymes are elevated, which, like, could be a million things? I literally looked it up. Ibuprofen can do that. Stress can do that. I've been insanely stressed. It doesn't automatically mean what everyone's decided it means. Everyone just wants a story.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When the doctor's office called... what was that moment like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? For like — five minutes I was scared. Actually scared. And then I just kind of shut it down. Opened Instagram, posted a story, had three hundred comments within an hour, and I was fine again. [quieter] But then the next morning I woke up at like four a.m. and just... lay there. Couldn't go back to sleep. Which is not a thing I do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Four in the morning. Lying there in the dark. [long pause] Something found you in that quiet that you couldn't scroll away from.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — [long pause] I just felt really tired. Not like sleepy-tired. Like... the other kind. The kind where you're tired of — [stops herself] I don't know. [laughs softly] I probably need more magnesium or something. Or to get off my phone before bed. That's probably it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You almost finished that sentence. 'Tired of —' [pause] I noticed you stopped yourself. That took something, letting it get that close.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: [long pause] Tired of pretending it's all great, I guess. Like every single night out is the best night ever. [quieter] It's exhausting, actually. But — [sits up straighter] I mean, that's just content creation. That's the job. Everyone performs a little. It's not like I'm lying.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean... if Kayla was right? If your mom was right? I'm not saying they are. I'm just wondering if you've let yourself go there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Then... [very long pause] I don't know who I am without it. That's the honest answer. Like, every memory I have that actually feels good, actually feels real — there's a drink in my hand. My followers, my income, my friend group, all of it. What do I do, just become the girl who orders sparkling water and posts about her wellness journey? [pause] God. That sounded so much sadder out loud than it did in my head.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to reflect back what I've heard today, if that's okay. [pause] You came in after one of the hardest weeks you've had in a while. You got a call from a doctor that scared you — really scared you, even if just for five minutes. You lay awake at four in the morning with something you couldn't name. And just now, you said out loud that you don't know who you are without it. [pause] You've been carrying all of that, and you still showed up here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: [quiet for a moment] Okay when you say it all like that it sounds... [exhales] Look, I'm not like — I'm not falling apart. I'm really not. But maybe — and I'm just thinking out loud here — maybe I could be a little more intentional? Like I don't have to drink at every single event. I could do like a 'mindful drinking month' or something. My followers would actually love that, which is — [laughs] I know, I know, I'm already making it content. But still.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: [soft laugh] You're already thinking about how to move through your world differently. [pause] I'm curious — what would one night look like? Not for the post. Just for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: [pause] Honestly? Probably kind of awkward. [laughs] I'd be standing there like, what do I do with my hands? Do I tell people? Do I just... not say anything and see if anyone even notices? [pause] But maybe that's okay. Maybe I can handle awkward for one night. [quieter] I'm not saying I have a problem. I want to be really clear about that. But being more... intentional. That feels like something I could actually do.

client_context: A 34-year-old artist who believes alcohol fuels creativity. Has been drinking daily for years. Recently noticed the art has gotten worse, not better.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, thanks for squeezing this in — I know you've got somewhere to be after this, so we'll work with whatever time we've got. What made you decide to come today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? My partner basically gave me an ultimatum. So. Here I am. I don't think I have like... a problem, but Marcus is convinced I do and he wouldn't let it go, so.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you're here partly because Marcus matters to you, even if you're not totally sold on the reason he sent you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean... I love him. But it's like — he doesn't get it. I'm an artist. I've been drinking wine while I paint since I was like twenty-two. That's just how I work. It loosens something up, you know? The inhibitions or whatever. I do my best stuff when I'm a little... relaxed.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The relaxed version of you — she's the artist. And you've built your whole process around that. I'm curious though, you mentioned the art has been off lately. What does the work actually look like right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I didn't — I don't know who told you that. Marcus, probably. Look, my process is mine. He's not an artist, he doesn't understand that it looks different for everyone, and it's really frustrating that everyone in my life is suddenly an expert on how I should be creating. Like, back off.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're protective of your process — that makes complete sense. It's yours, you built it. Setting Marcus aside entirely — what does the work feel like when you sit down with it these days, just for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... I don't know. It's been flat. I keep starting things and they just — they don't go anywhere. And I've actually been drinking more to try to get back to that flow state but it's like... the more I drink, the less it's coming. And I don't know what that means. It kind of scares me, actually.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you've been chasing that feeling — the one that used to unlock something — and the more you reach for it, the further away it gets. That's a really honest thing to notice about yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. ...Yeah. What if the drinking was never actually the thing? What if I just told myself that story so many times it became true in a way I didn't mean it to? God, that's a weird thought. I don't know if I'm ready to look at that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in rushed, a little reluctant, basically dragged here by someone you love — and in twenty minutes you just said something that takes a lot of people years to get to. The story you've been telling yourself might be costing you the very thing it was supposed to protect. That's not a small thing to sit with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...I need to think about that. I mean — I'm not saying I'm quitting tomorrow or whatever. But maybe. Maybe there's something here worth... looking at.

client_context: A 72-year-old with chronic pain who has been mixing alcohol with pain medication. Family is terrified. Doesn't want to burden anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hi Margaret — or do you prefer something else? I'm Dr. Chen. Thanks for joining me today. These telehealth calls can feel a little strange, talking to a screen. Just want you to know there's no rush, and you can be as honest as you like with me. So — what brought you here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Hello, yes, Margaret is fine. Um... I saw something — one of those health articles, on my phone. My daughter showed it to me, actually. I just thought maybe I should... talk to someone. I don't really do this sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm glad you made the call. Tell me a little more about what's been going on — what was it about that article that made it feel relevant to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well... I have arthritis. Pretty bad, in my hips and my lower back. Been like that for, oh, eight or nine years now. And the pain pills, they only do so much, you know? So I started having a glass of wine with dinner. Maybe two. It just takes the edge off. It's not — I mean, it's not a big deal. Lots of people have a glass of wine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the wine started as a way to handle what the medication wasn't quite touching — and it's become part of how you get through the day.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I suppose, yes. But — I don't want to make this into something it isn't — my daughter got very upset last month. She said she found me... I had taken my pills and then had three glasses and I was very out of it. She was scared. Which I don't want. She has enough to worry about already.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment clearly stayed with you — seeing your daughter that scared. What was it like for you when she told you what she found?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Awful. I felt just awful. I don't — that's not who I am. I've always been the one who took care of things. And now here I am and... I worry sometimes that maybe it's gotten a little out of hand. Just a little. But the pain is real. That part isn't made up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Nobody is saying the pain isn't real, Margaret. It is. And you've spent years managing it on your own, without making it anyone else's problem. That takes a quiet kind of strength.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yes. I don't like asking for help. Never have. But I'll be honest — and I don't know why I'm telling a stranger this — I've been frightened. Not every day, but sometimes I wake up at night and I think, what if something had really happened? What if I had fallen? My hip, if I fell...

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That fear is telling you something. When you imagine making a change — cutting back, finding another way through the pain — what worries you most about that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The pain. Plain and simple. Without the wine I don't — I don't know how I'd get through some nights. The pills aren't enough on their own. And I don't want more pills. At least wine is... it's natural. I know that sounds foolish.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound foolish. You've been trying to solve a real problem with the tools you had. And now you're sitting here wondering whether those same tools are starting to make things worse.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... yes. That's exactly it. I hadn't thought of it that way but — yes. Solving one thing and making another thing worse. I don't want to be sitting here in two years with a much bigger problem. I've seen that happen. A friend of mine, she — well. It went very badly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you is looking down the road. What does the version of Margaret who's handled this look like — a year from now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Someone who... who her daughter doesn't worry about. Who can have dinner with her grandchildren and actually be present for it. Not foggy. I want to be there — really there. I think I've been less there than I'd like to admit.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Margaret, let me try to pull together what I've heard today, if that's alright. You came in because something scared you — not just your daughter's fear, but your own. You've been managing serious, real pain the best way you knew how, and somewhere along the way it started to feel like it might be slipping out of your hands. You don't like needing help, never have, but you also don't want to become someone your family has to worry about — or lose real time with the people you love. And you're clear-eyed enough to see where this road goes if nothing changes.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it like that... yes. That's all of it. I've been dancing around it for months, I think. Maybe longer. I — I think I'm ready to actually do something. I just don't know what yet.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's enough — knowing you're ready. We don't need to solve everything today. But I'm curious: is there one small thing, just one, that feels like a possible place to start?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I could talk to my doctor. About the pain side of things. I've been afraid to bring it up because I didn't want her to take my medication away, but... maybe if there's another option I don't know about. And maybe — maybe I could tell my daughter that I talked to you today. That would mean a lot to her. I think it would mean a lot to me too.

client_context: A 21-year-old college senior who binge drinks every weekend. Friends staged an intervention but the student sees it as normal college behavior.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know walking into a place like this can feel... I don't know, maybe a little strange, especially if it wasn't exactly your idea. What's on your mind?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I don't really know why I'm here. My friends kind of... they did this whole thing last week and I guess I just came to get them off my back. I don't have a problem or anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So your friends were worried enough to sit you down and have a real conversation with you, and here you are. That matters, even if the whole thing felt like a lot.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah, I guess. It was kind of dramatic honestly. Like, everyone drinks in college. I go out on weekends, I have fun, I'm not like... failing my classes or anything. I don't see what the big deal is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm. What do you think it was that had them worried enough to actually do that? Your friends who know you well.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I don't know. Tyler said something about... I blacked out at his place a couple weeks ago and apparently I said some stuff I don't remember saying. But that happens to everyone, right? It's not like it's a pattern or...

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You said 'I don't remember'... and then you stopped. I'm just sitting with that for a second. What is it like, not knowing what you said that night?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... look, it's whatever. It's not like I hurt anyone. I just... sometimes I wonder what I said. Tyler's been kind of weird with me since then and he won't tell me. That's more his problem than mine though.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's something heavy about that gap you can't fill. And the way you said Tyler's name just now... it sounds like that friendship really means something to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...yeah. I mean, he's been my best friend for like three years. I don't... I don't want to lose that over some stupid night out. But I'm not going to stop drinking just because he got all sensitive about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You clearly care deeply about the people in your life. I'm curious - what do you want things to actually look like with Tyler, with your friends, a year from now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want things to go back to normal. Like, I want him to stop looking at me like I'm some kind of... I don't know. I'm applying to jobs, I've got stuff happening after graduation. I'm not some burnout. I have a future.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You see a real future for yourself. And it sounds like part of you is trying to figure out how everything fits together - the weekends, Tyler, who you want to be when you walk across that stage.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess... I never really thought about it like that. I've just kind of done what everyone else does and not really... I don't know. I still don't think I have a problem problem. But maybe... I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in today not knowing what to expect, and you sat with some things that weren't easy to look at - the gap in your memory, Tyler, what you actually want your life to look like. That takes something real.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... I'm not saying I'm going to like, quit drinking or whatever. That's not happening. But I guess I could... maybe think about some of this more. I don't know. Maybe I'll come back. We'll see.

client_context: A 29-year-old who moved to a new country alone and started drinking to cope with loneliness and cultural adjustment. Has no local support system.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for squeezing this in — I know you mentioned you're between classes. I want to make sure we use the time in a way that's actually useful for you. What brought you in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... the nurse said I had to come, basically. Something about my lab results being off — some enzyme thing. I don't know, I'm sure it's nothing. I've been really stressed with school, I haven't been sleeping well, it's probably just that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you got this letter and part of you is thinking — okay, probably not a big deal, there's an explanation for it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, I read what they sent. They flagged my liver enzymes. The doctor mentioned alcohol could be a factor but — a lot of things can cause that. Diet, medication, whatever. I don't take it as like... a diagnosis or anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Sure, there are several things that can affect those levels. I'm curious — what does drinking actually look like for you these days? Just to get a picture.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, I'm not drinking in the morning or anything like that. It's just — after class, at night, I'll have a few glasses of wine. Sometimes more. I moved here alone, I don't really have... I don't know anyone here yet. So it's just me in my apartment and it's really quiet and it helps me, like, turn my brain off. I don't think that makes me an alcoholic or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like drinking has become the thing that softens the silence — especially when you're far from home and the people who used to fill that space just... aren't there anymore.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. That's actually — yeah. Back home I was always with people. My family, my friends, we'd just be together, it was normal. Here it's just so quiet all the time. And sometimes the quiet gets really loud, if that makes sense? So I drink until I can sleep. I never really said it out loud like that before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to just acknowledge something — you came here today even though you're rushed, even though part of you wasn't sure it was necessary. That matters. And what you just described — building a whole life in a new country, completely on your own, without your support system — that is genuinely hard. It makes a lot of sense that you found something to get through it. It also sounds like a part of you has been quietly tracking this for a while.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... yeah. I tell myself it's fine, I'm handling it, but honestly? I'm scared about the lab results. And I'm also just — I'm really lonely. Like, a lot. And I don't want to keep doing this, I don't think this is actually helping me anymore. It just makes the next day harder.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't want to keep doing this. And underneath all of it — there's someone who's really missing connection. Who wants to actually be known by people here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I think that's it. There's actually an international students group I've seen flyers for, I keep walking past them and just... not doing it. Telling myself I'm too busy or it'll be weird. But maybe that's what I actually need. Like, more than the wine. I think I want to try — actually try.

client_context: A 38-year-old mandated by court to attend counseling after a second DUI. Furious about being forced to be here. Sees the system as unfair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know this isn't exactly where you wanted to be on a Thursday morning. And I just want you to know — whatever you're feeling right now, frustration, anger, whatever it is, that's okay here. This is your time. So... start wherever feels right.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Where feels right. [laughs bitterly] I'm here because a judge told me I had to be here. That's it. I don't have a — I don't have a 'drinking problem,' I had two bad nights, and now I'm supposed to sit here and talk about my feelings for what, twelve weeks? The whole system is a joke. I'm a working man. I pay my taxes. And I gotta sit here like I'm some kind of criminal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The system put you in this chair, and that feels completely unjust.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It IS unjust. My buddy — does the exact same thing, same stretch of road, gets a warning. Me? Two grand, license suspended, and now... this. I'm not saying what I did was — look, I'm not an idiot. But who decides who's the problem? You know? Like, who draws that line?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The rules felt like they landed on you in a way they didn't land on somebody else, and that's a hard thing to sit with. [pause] I also noticed — when you called to set this up, you mentioned some lab results your doctor flagged. I don't want to push, but... what's going on with that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My doctor said my liver enzymes were elevated. Sent me this letter, like, very clinical, 'please follow up.' [waves hand] I just got out of detox three days ago. Of course they're gonna be elevated. That's — I mean, that's normal, right? It doesn't necessarily mean anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: [quietly] It doesn't mean anything... and yet you're here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... [long pause] My ex used to say I'd die before I admitted I had a problem. I'm not saying she's right. But my dad — he died at fifty-two. Liver. And I watched that whole thing go down. Every stage of it. And I told myself I was never gonna be him, and now I'm... [trails off, shifts in chair] I don't know. I guess I just wanted to talk to someone who wasn't, like, court-appointed.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying your father with you this whole time. And it's sitting right underneath all of this, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't — I don't really talk about that. [pause] He was functional for a long time. Like, fine, totally fine, and then one day he just... wasn't. And I watched it. I watched the whole slide. And I swore I wasn't gonna do that, and somehow I'm — [voice drops] maybe I'm more like him than I ever wanted to admit.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does it mean to you — if that's true? That you're more like him than you thought?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It means... [swallows] I have a daughter. She's nine. I barely see her as it is — that's another whole thing — and if something happens to me... [pause] She doesn't deserve that. She deserves better than what I got. Better than watching someone disappear in front of her.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Even sitting in one of the hardest places you've been in a long time, she's the first thing you go to. That tells me something real about who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: [quiet, softer laugh] Yeah, well. I don't always act like it. That's kind of the problem. [pause] But yeah. She's... she's the whole thing. [looks down] I don't know if I can actually change. I've said I would before. But I'm here, right? I mean — that's something, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I've heard today, because I think it matters. You came in angry — and that makes complete sense. You were pushed into a room you didn't choose. But somewhere in this conversation, something else showed up. You talked about your dad, and what you watched him go through, and a promise you made to yourself. You talked about lab results that scared you, even if you're not fully ready to name that yet. And you talked about your daughter, and what you want her to have that maybe you didn't get. That's not nothing. That's actually... the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: [long pause] Yeah. [exhales slowly] I'm still pissed about the DUI thing. I'm not over that. But... okay. I hear you. I can — yeah. I'll come back. Let's keep going.

client_context: A 24-year-old PhD student who has been drinking to manage thesis stress and imposter syndrome. Advisor noticed declining work quality.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey Marcus, good to meet you. Glad you made it in today — and I mean that genuinely, not just as like a thing counselors say. So I usually like to start by just... hearing from you. No agenda yet. What's going on from your perspective?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I, um... I don't really know where to start, honestly. I just finished the detox thing last week and I'm still kind of... I feel like I'm moving through fog, you know? Like everything is just muted. I thought I'd feel better by now but I mostly just feel tired and kind of embarrassed to be here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Everything still feels muted. Like the world got quieter — but not necessarily in a good way.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. I mean I thought — I don't know, I guess I expected to feel clearer? But I just feel... empty, sort of. And my thesis is still a disaster. Like, the drinking stopped but the dissertation didn't fix itself overnight, so. I'm not sure what I actually solved.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a lot to sit with — the drinking's gone but the thing that was driving you toward it is still right there waiting for you. What does the dissertation situation actually look like for you right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... bad. I'm like two years behind on my timeline, my advisor basically put me on notice last month, and I just — I honestly don't know if I'm smart enough to finish this thing. I never did. I think I've been faking it since I got accepted and the drinking just made it easier to not think about that. Like, if I'm drunk I don't have to sit with the fact that I might just be... not cut out for this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That takes real guts to say out loud. Seriously — most people spend years not saying that part.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... is it guts or is it just giving up? Because sometimes it feels like I'm saying 'I'm not good enough' and then calling it self-awareness. I don't know if there's a difference anymore. ... Sorry. That probably made no sense.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No, it made complete sense. And it's a real question worth sitting with. So let me ask you this — when you imagine actually finishing, not just surviving the next week but actually defending this thing, what does that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... god. I used to have this whole picture, actually. Like defending, and then my parents flying in... my dad especially. He never went to college, like at all, worked construction his whole life. I used to think about him sitting in the audience when I defended and — ... I haven't thought about that in a really long time. That image kind of got buried somewhere.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It didn't disappear though. That image — your dad in those seats — that's still in there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it is. And that's actually... that's kind of why I finally checked myself in. I called home drunk one night, like really drunk, and he picked up and I could just hear it in his voice how worried he was. And I thought — I'm destroying the exact thing I'm supposedly doing all of this for. That was the moment. That was when I made the call.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull some of this together, because I think there's something real here. You came out of detox last week, things still feel foggy and raw, the thesis is still looming. And underneath all of that — underneath the imposter syndrome, the advisor pressure, all of it — there's this image you've been carrying for years. Your dad in that audience. A phone call that scared you enough to finally act. And despite everything, you're sitting in this chair right now. That didn't happen by accident.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it that way... yeah. I mean, I still don't know if I can actually do it. But I guess I'm... I don't know, I'm not completely giving up? I thought I was going to walk in here and just be like, I have no idea why I'm here. But I kind of do know. That's... something, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You know exactly why you're here. So — and take your time with this — what would one first step look like for you? Not the whole mountain. Just the next foothold.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... emailing my advisor. Just telling him I've been in treatment, that I'm serious about getting back on track. I've been avoiding it because I'm terrified of what he'll say, but I think hiding is making it worse. Like, the silence is its own problem at this point. That feels like the thing I can actually do this week.

client_context: An 18-year-old referred by school counselor after being caught drinking at a school event. Feels singled out since 'literally everyone drinks'.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back. That says something. Last week I got the sense this wasn't exactly where you wanted to be — how are you feeling about being here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I'm here, aren't I? My mom basically said it wasn't optional so. I still think this whole thing is kind of overkill for like, one incident.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You feel like the response has been way bigger than what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Like, I got caught at one party — one — and now I'm in counseling, my mom is watching me like a hawk, and the school literally has a file on me. But everyone was drinking that night. Everyone. I wasn't even that drunk.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And yet, even with all of that going on — your mom stressed, school involved, feeling singled out — you still walked through that door today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I... I don't know. I figured if I bailed it would make everything worse. And last time wasn't as bad as I thought. You didn't just lecture me the whole time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it have looked like if I had?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The same stuff everyone says. 'Drinking is bad, you could become an alcoholic, think about your future.' Like... I've heard it a thousand times. It doesn't actually do anything. It just makes me tune out.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The warnings have become noise. They stopped meaning anything a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Kind of, yeah. It's like... okay, I know the risks. I'm not stupid. It's just... I don't know, sometimes it's the only way to actually feel like I belong? Like people actually want me there? Is that... is that a weird thing to say?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Not weird at all. Wanting to belong is one of the most human things there is. Tell me more about that — what does it feel like when it's working? When you're out, you've had a few drinks, and things feel easy?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... actually really good. Like the anxiety just kind of goes away. I'm not in my head about every single thing I say, I'm not wondering if people actually like me or they're just tolerating me. I just feel... normal. Easy. Like I can breathe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So underneath all of this — the party, getting caught, all the fallout — there's been a lot of anxiety that you've been carrying around for a while.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. I guess. I don't really talk about that part. It sounds weak. My friend group isn't exactly the type where you'd be like, 'hey guys I have a lot of anxiety and drinking makes it stop.' They'd think I was so weird.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you've been handling this completely alone. Carrying the anxiety, figuring out how to manage it, doing it in a way that keeps you in with your friends — all without being able to say out loud what's actually going on for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that it sounds... really lonely. And it kind of is, I think. I didn't think it was before but... yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That takes so much energy. And you've been doing it for a while, by the sounds of it. Is there any part of you that's tired of it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Honestly... yeah. I'm tired of dreading Monday because I'm scared I said something embarrassing at the party. Or waking up and not totally remembering what happened and just waiting to see if I did something stupid. That part really sucks. Like that's not... that's not actually fun.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just named something really important. The thing that's supposed to take the pressure off is creating its own kind of pressure. And you saw that yourself — I didn't point it out, you got there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never... huh. Yeah. I never really thought about it like that before. Like it's supposed to be the solution but then there's this whole other thing to stress about after. That's kind of messed up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If the anxiety is the real thing — the thing underneath all of this — what might it actually look like to deal with that? Not push it down, but actually work on it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Like... therapy, maybe? Talking to someone about it. Which I guess is kind of what this is, actually. I don't know if I'd even know how to hang out with people without drinking being part of it, but... maybe that's something I could figure out. Maybe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing across today. You came in feeling like this whole thing was blown out of proportion — and maybe part of you still feels that way. But somewhere in this conversation you started talking about something real: anxiety you've been carrying alone for a long time, a way of coping that comes with its own cost, and the beginning of something that sounds like being ready to try something different. You didn't have to go there. But you did.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. I did, didn't I. I don't know what I'm doing yet or whatever. But... yeah. Maybe this is actually the right place to try to figure it out.

client_context: A 21-year-old college senior who binge drinks every weekend. Friends staged an intervention but the student sees it as normal college behavior.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in. I know the first time walking through that door can feel a little... weird. Just so you know, nothing you say here surprises me — I've heard a lot. So, what brought you in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh... honestly? My friends. They did this whole, like, intervention thing last weekend and I just — look, I figured if I came in once, they'd chill out and stop treating me like I'm some kind of addict or whatever. I'm not. I'm a college student. That's what we do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So being here is more about getting some peace than because you think something's actually wrong.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. I mean... I don't know, like, maybe there's a tiny part of me that — no, whatever. It's fine. Most of my friends don't really drink, so when they see me having a good time they just, like, freak out. That's on them. I'm not gonna apologize for having fun.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about last weekend. What actually happened that got people concerned enough to say something?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It wasn't a big deal. I had some drinks at this party — more than usual, okay, sure — and I guess I got into it with some guy, and... I don't remember all of it, honestly. But apparently I scared some people. Which is stupid because everyone was wasted, I wasn't the only one drinking. They're acting like I need to go to, like, AA or something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't remember all of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I mean, that happens when you drink a lot. That's just — that's normal, right? It's not like I black out every weekend. Just sometimes. And I still got home fine, I wasn't in a ditch somewhere, so. It's not like I'm some kind of mess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're already asking yourself 'is this normal?' — even while you're telling me it's fine. That's not nothing. Most people wouldn't even let themselves go there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I guess. Look, I'm not worried about myself. But my girlfriend — she said she's scared of me when I drink. And that's... I don't know. That one kind of got to me. I don't want her to be scared of me. That's not — that's not who I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you came in to get your friends off your back. But then you're describing a blackout that scared people, a confrontation you can't fully piece together, and your girlfriend telling you she's afraid of you when you drink. And underneath all the 'it's not a big deal' — what I'm hearing is that you actually care a lot about who she sees when she looks at you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I do. She matters to me. I just — I'm not swearing off drinking forever, like, that's not gonna happen. But maybe I could... I don't know. Figure something out. I'm not making any promises. But maybe.

client_context: A 24-year-old PhD student who has been drinking to manage thesis stress and imposter syndrome. Advisor noticed declining work quality.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm Dr. Reyes. I know walk-ins can feel a little uncertain — you're not sure what you're walking into. So just so you know, there's no agenda here, no checklist. What brought you in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh... yeah. Um. My friend basically dragged me here. Not literally, but — she was really worried and I just didn't have a good reason to say no, I guess. So here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She cared enough that you felt like you couldn't push back. What's been going on lately that got her worried?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it's not like I have a problem or anything. It's just been a rough semester. My thesis isn't going well, my advisor basically told me my last chapter draft was — his words — 'not PhD-level work.' So yeah, I've been drinking more at night just to unwind. But it's not a big deal, it's just stress.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: On top of the already crushing pressure of a dissertation, you got that feedback from your advisor. And drinking became how you get through the night.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And honestly... I don't even know if 'unwind' is the right word anymore. It's more like I just — stop feeling it for a while. The doubt. The... I'm seriously starting to wonder if I belong in this program at all. Like maybe my advisor is right. Maybe I'm just not cut out for this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really heavy thing to be carrying. Feeling like maybe you don't belong somewhere you fought hard to get into. When you imagine the version of yourself that actually finishes this PhD... what does that look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... God. I used to think about that all the time. I had this whole thing mapped out — finish the dissertation, maybe do a postdoc, eventually teach. I really wanted to teach. But lately I can't even picture it. It feels so far away that I've kind of just... stopped trying to see it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That vision didn't disappear. It got buried. And the drinking has been one way to get through the nights when it feels completely unreachable.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. And — I know it's not helping. Like, I wake up and I still have to open the same document I couldn't write the night before. It's just easier in the moment. But the mornings are getting worse and I know that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say the mornings are getting worse?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Foggy. Just... slow. I've been skipping my morning read-throughs because I can't focus. I missed a meeting with my advisor last week because I genuinely could not get it together in time. And that's — okay, yeah, saying it out loud, that's probably not great.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just named something important. The thing that was supposed to help you cope is now costing you in the exact place that matters most — your work, your relationship with your advisor, the PhD itself. Those aren't separate anymore.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it that way... yeah. I knew it, but I hadn't let myself actually think it. I've been treating them like two different problems. But they're not, are they.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something's shifting for you right now — I can hear it. What feels different about seeing that connection?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It actually makes me feel... less hopeless? Which is weird to say. But if the drinking is part of what's making the thesis worse, then I have some control over something. Instead of just being fundamentally bad at this. That's — that actually means something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing. You came in not knowing what to expect, carrying this really painful belief that maybe you don't belong in your program. Drinking started as relief from that — but you can see now it's feeding the cycle, not breaking it. And through all of it, there's still this part of you that wants to finish, wants to teach. That part hasn't gone anywhere.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's kind of exactly it. I think I needed to hear it back. I've been so deep in my own head that I couldn't see any of it clearly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've done a lot of honest work today for someone who wasn't even sure they wanted to be here. Given everything you just figured out — what's one thing you'd want to be different by the time we talk again?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... not drinking on nights before I have writing blocked out. That feels like something I could actually do. And showing up to my next advisor meeting instead of bailing. I think — yeah. I think I want to try.

client_context: A 72-year-old with chronic pain who has been mixing alcohol with pain medication. Family is terrified. Doesn't want to burden anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Well, come on in — have a seat. I promise that chair's more comfortable than it looks. [small laugh] I'm Sarah. So. First session after getting through detox. That's genuinely no small thing. How are you holding up today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I didn't want to come here. My daughter practically dragged me. I'm fine — I was fine. A little wine in the evenings, that's all it ever was. People are acting like I was... I don't know. Like I was some sort of... it's just ridiculous. I'm 72 years old.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So everyone around you made a much bigger deal out of this than you think it deserved. And there's something humiliating about that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. I raised three children. I buried a husband. I've lived through things these doctors with their little clipboards couldn't even imagine. And suddenly my family's calling everyone, checking me into a — [shakes head] It's humiliating. That's exactly the word. I'm not a drunk. I've never been a drunk.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That word really doesn't fit how you see yourself — and I hear that. Can I ask you something? In your own words... what do you think was actually going on? With the drinking and the pain medication together?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Nobody tells you what it's really like. Getting old. Everything hurts — my back, my hip, and the pills they give you barely... they barely touch it. So yes, I'd have a drink. It helped me sleep. It helped me get through the day without calling my daughter every five minutes about how much pain I was in. I live alone. I wasn't hurting anyone. I was just — [stops herself] I'm sorry. I know that sounds like I'm making excuses.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Don't apologize. Please. What I'm hearing is that you were carrying something enormous — serious pain, alone, every single day — and you found something that helped you manage it quietly so the people you love wouldn't have to worry. That's not an excuse. That's actually... that tells me a lot about who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just don't want to be a burden to them. That's... that's the whole thing, really. They have their own lives. Grandchildren, mortgages, all of it. My daughter already worries too much as it is. I thought if I could just manage quietly... [long pause] The detox was harder than I expected. I won't lie to you. I didn't realize how much I'd come to depend on it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just make sure I'm with you. You've been managing real, chronic pain mostly on your own — because you didn't want to add to anyone's plate. The alcohol helped you cope with that, at least for a while, until it started to become something your body needed. And now you're here, not exactly thrilled about it, but you did show up. And the detox — that was genuinely hard work.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. That's — yeah. [quiet] I didn't think I was dependent. I truly didn't. I thought I was just coping. And I suppose I was, just... not in a very good way. Not a safe way. I can see that now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That kind of honesty — especially right after something as hard as detox — that's not nothing. I want you to know that. So let me ask you this: what would actually taking care of yourself look like? Not for your daughter, not for your doctor. For you. What would that even mean?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I'm not sure I know. [small laugh] I've spent so long taking care of everyone else, I don't think I've ever really sat with that question. [pause] Maybe that's where we start. I don't know what it looks like yet. But I'm willing to find out. I'm here, aren't I?

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Come on in, have a seat. I appreciate you making time — I know you mentioned you've got somewhere else to be. Just want you to know there's no agenda here, no judgment. So, what's been going on for you lately?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, uh... my doctor sent me. Said I had to come talk to somebody. I wasn't really planning on it but my daughter sort of — you know how it is — she made sure I showed up. So. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your doctor referred you and your daughter made sure you followed through. I'm curious — when those lab results came back, what was that like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: They flagged some numbers. Liver stuff. And the doctor's going on and on about it like I'm some kind of — I don't know, like I'm some alcoholic off the street. I have a couple drinks in the evening. That's it. I worked for forty years. I think I've earned a glass of scotch at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the doctor's reaction felt way out of proportion to what you're actually doing. Like he turned it into something bigger than it really is.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. What does he know about my life? I'm retired. I'm alone most of the day. What am I supposed to do — sit there and watch the news? My wife passed three years ago and... look, the drinking isn't the problem. The problem is I've got nothing to do. Nobody telling me I'm needed anywhere.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes something to say that out loud. Losing your wife, retiring, going from a full life to just... quiet. That's real loss. And it makes complete sense that you'd find something to fill that space.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's not filling a space. It's just what I do now. I'm not hurting anybody. I don't drive after. I just — it helps me sleep, okay? I'm not gonna apologize for that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't have to apologize at all. I'm just wondering — and you can be completely honest with me — what made you actually walk through that door today? Because you didn't have to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The... the numbers were pretty bad. Doctor said if they don't improve by the next checkup we're talking about, uh... possible liver damage. He used that word. Damage. And I'm 65, not 85. I've got... I mean, I'd like to think I've still got years ahead of me. So. That scared me a little. More than a little, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That word — damage — that landed differently. Like this stopped being just numbers on a page.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah it did. My wife had health problems the last two years and I... I watched her go through it. I know what it looks like when things start going wrong and doctors start using certain words. I don't want to be that guy. I don't want to end up in some hospital bed wondering why I didn't do something sooner.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That image — being that guy — clearly means something to you. Can I ask, before all of this... before the drinking picked up, what did your days look like? What gave you structure?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I was an electrician for... thirty-eight years. Foreman the last twelve. Every day I had a crew, I had a job, people depending on me. Then I retired and it's like the phone just stopped ringing. My buddies are still working or moved away. Kids have their own lives. And it's just me and the TV and... yeah. I didn't expect it to feel like this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I'm putting this together right. You spent almost four decades with purpose, structure, people depending on you — and retirement took all of that away faster than you expected. Then you lost your wife. And somewhere in there, the drinking became a way to get through the evenings, get some sleep, feel a little less alone. And now the lab results are telling you the one thing you have left — your health — might be slipping too. Does that feel close?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's pretty much it. When you say it like that it sounds kind of bad. I didn't see it happening. It just sort of crept up on me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It crept up. What worries you most if things just keep going the way they are — another year from now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I'm worried I'll just... disappear. Not die, just — shrink. Become someone my kids are embarrassed by. Or worse, someone they have to take care of. I don't want that. I raised them to be independent. I want to be independent too. And I'm not stupid — I know what I'm doing to myself isn't helping. I know that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That kind of honesty — being able to see what's happening and still caring enough about yourself, about your kids, to say it out loud — that's not a small thing. You came in today. You sat with some hard stuff. And you told me the truth. That matters more than you probably realize.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm not ready to throw out the bottles or anything like that. But... I think I need to figure something out. The retirement, the being alone, and yeah — the drinking. This isn't working. Something's gotta change. I just don't know where to start.

client_context: A 24-year-old PhD student who has been drinking to manage thesis stress and imposter syndrome. Advisor noticed declining work quality.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in. I know walking into a new place takes something. So — what's going on for you right now? What brought you here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh... honestly I'm not totally sure. I saw something about this clinic online and I just... I don't know. Things have been rough for a while and I kind of hit a wall this week.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A wall. Tell me more about that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: So I'm a third-year PhD student — computational biology — and my advisor pulled me in last week and basically told me my last two chapters read like I wasn't really there. Which... he's right. And I've been drinking more than I probably should be and I know that. I know that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you already knows something's off — and hearing it from your advisor made it harder to keep that at arm's length.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... I don't know if I'd call it a problem exactly. Like I can stop when I want to. But I've seen counselors before and it never really went anywhere, so I'm kind of... I guess I'm skeptical this is going to be different. No offense.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No offense taken — that's a fair thing to bring in. Something kept you trying though. You're here. What felt different about this week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm... I'm the first person in my family to go to grad school. Like, ever. And sitting there in my advisor's office feeling like a complete fraud, I just thought — what am I doing? I worked so hard to get here and I'm just... I'm blowing it. And that scared me more than anything has in a long time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You carried yourself into a program most people never get to, and you're still holding yourself to that standard even when everything feels like it's slipping. That matters. And it sounds like the drinking is tangled up in all of this — the stress, the fear. How did it start?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It started because I couldn't sleep. Like, thesis anxiety, two a.m., brain just wouldn't stop. And a couple drinks helped. And then it became the thing I did after every bad day. And now... bad days are kind of every day, so. Yeah. It's just there all the time now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What started as a fix has become part of the problem.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And I hate that. I genuinely hate it. I had friends in undergrad who had drinking problems and I always thought — I'll see it if it happens to me. But I did see it. I just kept going anyway. That's the part I can't really explain.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: In that moment when you pour a drink — what does it actually give you? What does it do?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It... turns the volume down. There's this voice, like, you don't belong here, everyone else has it figured out, you're going to get found out — and the drinking just... quiets it. For a little while.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It gives you relief from something that feels relentless. And then morning comes.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: And then morning comes and the voice is louder and I'm hungover and I haven't done anything and... god. It doesn't actually help at all. I know that. I've known that for months. Intellectually I completely know that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That kid who was the first in his family to get here — the one who earned his spot in that lab — what would it mean for him if you found a way to quiet that voice without the drinking?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... um. That's a big question. I think... I think I'd actually have a real shot at finishing this thing. Because the work isn't bad. When I'm clear-headed and I'm actually in it, I'm good — I know I'm good. It's just I've been so rarely clear-headed lately that I've kind of... forgotten that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing. You came in here on your own — nobody pushed you through that door. You've already drawn the line between the drinking and the cycle you're stuck in. You know the work is in you. And there's a version of yourself — clear-headed, capable — who you haven't been able to reach in a while. That's a lot of clarity for a first session with someone you weren't sure you trusted.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. When you put it like that. I haven't really let myself say any of this out loud before. Usually I just tell myself I'm fine and then I drink and then I tell myself I'm fine again.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Not a huge overhaul — just this week. What's one thing that feels real and actually doable?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe just... tracking it. Being honest with myself about the actual number, because I think I've been deliberately not knowing. And maybe texting my friend Marcus — he went through something similar a couple years ago. I know he'd pick up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You walked in here today. And just now you named two concrete things — without me suggesting either one. I think you already know more about what you need than you've been giving yourself credit for.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Maybe. I mean... I don't think this is going to be easy. But for the first time in a while I feel like — I don't know — like maybe I don't have to figure all of this out drunk. That probably sounds dumb.

client_context: A 37-year-old middle school teacher who drinks every evening and occasionally comes to work hungover. A colleague noticed and expressed concern privately.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I want you to know there's no agenda here on my end — I'm just interested in hearing from you. Can you tell me, in your own words, what brought you in?

utterances.speaker: client
