utterances.text: Uh, yeah. So my doctor ran some bloodwork a few weeks ago — just a routine physical, nothing dramatic — and some of the numbers came back off. Liver stuff, she said. She mentioned maybe cutting back on drinking and, um... suggested I talk to someone. So. Here I am, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the lab results were enough of a jolt that it felt worth showing up today — even if you're not totally sure what to make of being here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. It was a little alarming, honestly. But I want to be clear — I'm not like, a big drinker. It's just, I have a drink in the evenings to unwind. Teaching middle schoolers is... it's a lot. You know? It helps me decompress. I don't think that makes me some kind of alcoholic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Teaching middle school — that's genuinely exhausting work. I'd like to get a better picture of what a typical evening actually looks like for you. What's kind of your usual routine when you get home?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I get home, make dinner, maybe watch something. And yeah, I'll have a few beers. Sometimes wine. It's not like I'm doing shots or anything crazy. Three, four drinks maybe. Sometimes a bit more on the weekend. But I'm functional — I get up, I go to work, I do my job. I'm not stumbling around.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So on one hand, you've got this routine that genuinely helps you come down after hard days — and you see yourself as someone who keeps it together, who shows up. And on the other hand, those lab results are kind of sitting there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Like — I do keep it together. Most of the time. I mean... there have been mornings where I felt, uh, not great. But everyone has off mornings. That's just... that's life. I'm not an alcoholic, if that's what this is heading toward.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I hear you — and I want to be clear, I'm not here to put a label on anything. What I'm noticing is that you're someone who takes his work seriously and is carrying a lot. I'm curious though — when you say mornings where you feel 'not great,' what does that actually look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Just... tired. Headache sometimes. There was one day last month where a colleague — Sarah — she said I looked pale and asked if I was okay in front of like three other teachers. That was... that was embarrassing. I brushed it off, said I wasn't sleeping well. But... I don't know. It stuck with me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me make sure I'm following. You came in today because of the lab results, not really because you think drinking is a problem. At the same time, there are these moments — mornings you feel rough, a colleague noticing something — that you haven't quite been able to shake. And there's a part of this that's sitting uncomfortably, even if you're not sure what to do with it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I guess that's... that's fair. I mean, I wasn't even going to come here. My wife doesn't know I'm here. I told her it was a follow-up appointment with the doctor.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took something — coming in without anyone knowing. What made you actually decide to walk through the door today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The doctor had this look on her face. She wasn't panicking or anything, but she wasn't casual about it either. And I kept thinking... I'm 37. I've got two kids. I can't — I mean, I don't want to...

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't want this to be the thing that catches up with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. I watched my dad — he was a drinker. Not like, abusive or anything. He just kind of... checked out. And I swore I wouldn't be that. But lately I've been wondering if maybe I'm more like him than I thought. That's a hard thing to say.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you think about the kind of father — the kind of person — you want to be, what does that look like to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Someone who's actually present. Not just physically in the room. My son — he's nine — he's doing soccer now and I've missed a lot of practices. I always have a reason. But honestly... a lot of evenings I'm just zoned out on the couch. I don't even really remember what we talked about at dinner.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just connected something really important — you linked the drinking to something that actually matters to you. A lot of people never get there, especially not in a first conversation. That's significant.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. I haven't said any of this out loud before. It's weird, hearing it. I still don't know if I have like, a problem problem. But... maybe something has gotten out of hand a little. Maybe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You said 'maybe something has gotten out of hand.' If you were to take one small step — something that felt real and actually doable — what might that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... not drinking on weeknights? Like actually try, not just tell myself I'm going to and then open a beer anyway. I honestly don't know if I can do it. But I think I'd like to find out. Does that sound stupid?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Not at all. Let me reflect back what I'm hearing across our whole conversation. You came in today not really convinced there was a problem — just following up on some lab results. And somewhere in here, something shifted. You started talking about your dad, about soccer practices you've missed, about evenings you can't quite account for. You're not ready to say this is a crisis, and I'm not asking you to. But you're starting to ask whether the way things are now is actually working for you. And you're willing to find out what you're capable of. That's a real starting point.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that... that feels right. I'm still not saying I need to like, never drink again or go to meetings or whatever. But I think I want to come back. I actually want to talk about this more. Which I did not expect to say walking in here.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again, Marcus. I'm glad you came back. ... How have things been since we last spoke?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Fine. Look, I want to be upfront — I'm only here because HR basically told me I had to be. I don't think I have some kind of... problem. I had a bad day, it got blown way out of proportion, and now I'm sitting here. So.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're being straight with me right from the start. That takes something. And even with all of that... you still came back.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. Whatever. It's not like I was drinking on the job or anything. Maybe I had a couple beers the night before and I was a little off the next morning. But every single guy I served with drinks. That's just — that's the culture, man. You come home, you decompress, nobody bats an eye over there. So excuse me if I don't see why it's suddenly such a massive deal back here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Drinking was part of how you and the guys got through it. A way to decompress after carrying all of that. And now you're home, and the same thing that was just... normal over there, gets you called into HR.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Thank you. Nobody gets that. My wife, my supervisor — none of them served, none of them get it. You'd have a drink and move on, you didn't sit around processing your feelings. And now I'm supposed to just flip a switch. Be a civilian overnight. ... She keeps saying I've changed. Like, yeah. Yeah I have. That happens when you've seen what I've seen.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She says you've changed. ... What do you think she means by that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She says I'm checked out. Not present. That the kids... um. That the girls barely see me even when I'm sitting right there. ... She said last month — she actually said it — that if things don't change she's done. Like, done done. Took them to her mom's for a week. That was... that was a rough week.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That week alone in the house... it sounds like it hit you in a way that was hard to shake.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was quiet. Too quiet. I'd sit there in the evenings and I'd just... start thinking. About everything. The deployment. Coming back. And I guess I started wondering if maybe I'm not handling things as well as I think I am. I'm not saying I have a problem. But maybe things have gotten a little... I don't know. Off track or something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me make sure I'm hearing you. You came back here today — even when part of you didn't want to — because somewhere in that quiet week, something in you started asking questions. About where things are heading. About your girls. About your wife. You're not ready to call it a problem. But something in you is paying attention.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. ... Yeah, that's — yeah. I can't lose my family. That's not an option for me. No matter what else is going on, those girls need their dad. And I want to be the kind of dad they actually deserve, you know? So... I don't know. Maybe I'm willing to look at some things. I'm not saying anything's wrong. But... maybe.

client_context: A 50-year-old who was sober for 3 years but relapsed after a sudden job loss. Feels deep shame and hopelessness. Has been to AA before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to meet you. I know the last few days have been... a lot. ER, then detox, and now you're sitting here. I'm not in any hurry. What brings you in today, in your own words?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? The hospital said I had to come or they wouldn't discharge me. I've done this before. AA, the steps, the whole thing. I know the drill. So... here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been through this before, and part of you is already bracing for it to be the same thing all over again.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Three years. I had three years sober. Three years. And then everything just... I don't even know how to explain it. It went sideways fast.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Three years is real. That didn't disappear. What happened when things started to unravel?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What happened. Twenty-two years at the same company. Twenty-two years. They walked me out with a cardboard box and a handshake. That's what happened. Like I was nothing. Like none of it meant anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Twenty-two years. That's not just a job — that was your identity, your structure, your whole routine. And they just... cut it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly! That's exactly it and nobody — my wife keeps saying 'you'll find something else, you're talented.' I'm fifty years old. I'm not gonna just find something else. I lost — I don't even know what I lost. Everything I built. Gone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: In that moment, drinking made sense. Like it was the only thing left that could hold you up.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... and then I'm lying in a hospital bed at two in the morning thinking, what am I doing. I had my chip. My sponsor — God, I haven't even called him. I can't. I don't know how to look at him.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What makes it hard to pick up the phone?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Because he was proud of me. They all were. I was the guy in the meeting who made it, you know? The one who gave people hope. And now I'm just... I'm back to being nobody. Less than nobody, because I knew better.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me make sure I'm hearing all of this. You lost your job — twenty-two years, your whole sense of who you were professionally. You lost your footing, and the relapse happened fast. And now on top of the grief and the physical wreckage, you're carrying this enormous shame. Like you failed the people who were counting on you. That's... a staggering amount to be holding all at once.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you lay it out like that... I don't know. I didn't drink because I wanted to. I know how that sounds but it's true. It was like I was drowning and that was the only way I knew to come up for air. But it didn't even work. It just made everything worse and I still had to wake up and deal with all of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You know what three years felt like. You've lived it. What would it mean to find your way back to that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think about my daughter. She was fifteen when I got sober. She's eighteen now and she told me once — she said 'Dad, you're the dad I always wanted.' And I just... I need to be that again. I don't know if I can get back there but I have to try. I have to.

client_context: A 33-year-old social media influencer whose entire social life revolves around drinking. Multiple friends have expressed concern. Insists it's just her lifestyle.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hi, I'm really glad you came in. I know you're squeezed for time today, so I just want you to know there's no agenda here. We can just... talk.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, I'll be honest — I'm not totally sure why I'm here. Dr. Patel kind of insisted, and I have a 2 PM lecture and then a brand call after that, so. I'm a little all over the place.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like today is already a lot. What's your sense of what Dr. Patel was hoping you'd get out of coming here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I think she just doesn't get my life. Like, I'm a content creator. Going out, being seen at events, having a drink in my hand at a rooftop — that's not a problem, that's literally my job. That's how I built my following.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the socializing, the nightlife, the drinking — it's all woven into who you are professionally. It's not separate from your work, it IS your work.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Do you know how many brand deals come through because someone spotted me at the right place? I show up, I look good, I have fun, I post it. The algorithm rewards consistency. This is how I pay rent. I'm not just, like, partying irresponsibly — I'm working.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That makes complete sense. I'm curious — you mentioned a few friends have expressed some concern. What was it like hearing that from them?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Ugh. It's annoying, honestly. Sarah calls me up like, 'I'm worried about you,' but she's literally the one texting me every weekend asking me to get her on guest lists. And Marcus — okay, Marcus doesn't drink at all so of course everyone looks like they have a problem to him. They're projecting. It's like, mind your business.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It feels like they want to be part of your world, but then they turn around and judge you for living it. Like they don't quite get to have it both ways.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes! Exactly. And it's — it's so frustrating because I have worked so hard to build what I have. I'm not stumbling around, I'm not losing jobs, I'm not missing deadlines. I am thriving. So what is the actual problem? Like what is everyone so worked up about?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've built something real. That takes discipline and hustle that most people don't see. And I hear you — from the outside and from the inside, things look like they're working.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Thank you. Yeah. I mean... mostly. Like. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I noticed you said 'mostly.' I don't want to put words in your mouth at all — but I'm wondering, are there ever moments, even small ones, where something feels a little... off?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... okay, there are mornings where I feel kind of rough. But like, that's everyone. That's just, you know, you stay out late, you feel it the next day. That's not — I'm not saying anything is wrong. I just need an extra coffee sometimes. That's normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There are mornings where your body is telling you something. And you notice it — even if you're not sure yet what it means.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess... there was this one thing. Last month I had a campaign shoot, and I'd gone out the night before, and I just — I kept blanking. Forgetting the angles we'd agreed on. The photographer had to redo so many shots and I could tell she was annoyed and I just felt so... I don't know. Off. Really embarrassed actually.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just gently reflect back what I'm hearing, because I want to make sure I understand. You love your life — the events, the community, the platform you've worked so hard to build. And at the same time, there are mornings that are harder than you'd like, and at least one moment where the night before got in the way of something that really mattered to you professionally. And the people who care about you are worried enough to say something out loud. I'm not drawing any conclusions — I'm just holding all of that alongside you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it all together like that it sounds... I don't know. Look, I want to be really clear — I'm not an alcoholic. That's not what's happening here. I just like having a good time. There's a difference between someone who enjoys their life and someone who has a problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Of course. And I hear you — that distinction feels important. Can I ask you something a little different? If everything went the way you hope, what does your life look like five years from now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I want bigger things. Like actual TV, maybe a product line. I want people to take me seriously as a businesswoman. Not just as like, the fun girl who's always at the party. I want... more than that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a version of you — a businesswoman, someone taken seriously on her own terms — that feels a little different from the image you're living right now. Like you can see her, but she's not quite... here yet.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I think about that sometimes. Like, how long can I actually keep this up. There are influencers who just kind of fade, you know? And I wonder sometimes if I'm building something real or if I'm just... partying until the algorithm moves on. I don't say that out loud usually.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That kind of honesty with yourself — about what you really want, about the fear underneath all of it — that takes a lot of courage to even let yourself think. I'm glad you said it out loud today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've never actually said that to anyone before. It's kind of... huh. I'm not ready to like, blow up my whole life or anything. I'm really not. But maybe... maybe there's something worth actually looking at. I don't know. Maybe.

client_context: A 20-year-old star athlete whose performance has been slipping due to partying. Coach gave an ultimatum. Torn between team loyalty and social life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for making it in today. I know you just finished the detox program — that's only a few days behind you. Before we get into anything, I just want to ask: what's going through your mind right now, being here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I don't really want to be here. No offense. Coach said I either get evaluated or I'm off the starting lineup, so... here I am. I'm not like — I don't think I'm an alcoholic or anything like that. I just had a bad stretch.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you is here because you had to be, and another part is already pushing back on what this whole thing even means about you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. Everyone's acting like I'm some kind of problem case now. I showed up to a morning lift a little off one time — okay, it was twice — but like... I've been playing ball since I was eight. My whole life is that team. That's not a drinking problem, that's just stress. A lot of guys do way worse.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've put everything into this sport — eight years old, that's a long time. I want to ask you something, and I don't want you to sugarcoat it: what was it actually like going through the detox this past week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was... [pause] rough. Like I didn't sleep almost at all. My hands wouldn't stop shaking the first two days. I kept telling myself it was just anxiety or dehydration, but the doctor said — she said my body was dependent. Which I just... I didn't know it had gotten to that point. I really didn't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Finding out your body was further down the road than you realized — and you stayed anyway. A lot of people walk out the first night.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I almost did. First night I was like, screw this. But then I thought about — [stops] ...my mom drove four hours to drop me off. She didn't say anything, she just hugged me in the parking lot for a really long time. And I couldn't just leave after that. I couldn't do that to her.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's actually at stake for you right now — beyond your mom, beyond the coach — if you're being honest with yourself?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Everything, man. Like... [long pause] I had scouts at two games this year. Division one interest, maybe a pro track somewhere down the line. And my numbers have been falling off since November. My coach, he's not a bad guy — he's just watched me throw away something kids would kill for. And I know that. I know that and I still kept going out.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You can see it slipping — something you've spent your whole life building. And some part of you knows what's been driving that slide.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. [quietly] I don't like saying that out loud. It started as like a reward thing after games — win, go out, celebrate. But then we'd lose and I'd still go out. And then it didn't even matter what happened. I'd just... it became the thing I looked forward to more than the game itself. And that's — that's not who I want to be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If the drinking just wasn't part of the picture — what does your life actually look like? Like, what does a good day feel like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Waking up not dreading practice. Going hard in the gym and actually feeling something, you know? Last fall I had this stretch — like six weeks — where everything was dialed in. Sleep, train, study, film. I felt like I was building toward something real. I want that back. I don't know if I can get it back, but... I want it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me pull together what I'm hearing — stop me if I get it wrong. You came in today under pressure, not convinced you needed to be here. But you got through something genuinely hard this week, and your mom being there mattered more than you expected. You know what's at risk with your career, you've already lived what it feels like when you're locked in, and underneath the 'I'm fine' stuff there's a part of you that wants that version of yourself back.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. That's pretty much it. [pause] It sounds more serious when someone else says it. Like I've been kind of — I think I've been running from how serious it actually is. For a while now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What feels like one thing you could actually do — not a big overhaul, just something real — between now and the next time we meet?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Tell my roommate what's actually going on. He's been covering for me with some of the guys and I think I've been isolating without even realizing it. If he knows the real situation — not the version I've been spinning — maybe I stop pretending everything's fine. And maybe I actually show up to these sessions instead of finding an excuse not to.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's not a small thing — choosing honesty over keeping up the front. You walked in here today not wanting to be here, and you're leaving with something concrete you're willing to do. That matters.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [small exhale] I'm still scared. Like I don't know what recovery even looks like for me as an athlete — I don't know if I can do this without it messing with my game somehow. But... I'm here. And I guess that's something.

client_context: A 26-year-old software engineer with severe social anxiety who uses alcohol as liquid courage at every social event. Knows it's a crutch but terrified of life without it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it's good to see you again. How have things been going since we last talked?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... okay, I guess. Like, mostly okay. I actually had a pretty good couple of weeks and then... yeah, it kind of fell apart a little last weekend.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So things were going well for a stretch, and then something shifted last weekend.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. My coworkers did this whole after-work thing — like a birthday happy hour — and I just... I knew I was gonna go and I was already anxious about it days before. And I told myself I'd have one or two drinks, but...

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What happened once you were there?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I had like five or six. Which isn't even the worst I've ever done, but I felt really bad about it after. Because I'd actually done well — two weekends in a row where I barely drank at all. And then one work thing and it just... reset everything, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're hard on yourself about Friday, and I get that. But I want to stay with what you just said — two weekends in a row. That's real. That didn't disappear.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah, I guess. It just doesn't feel like it matters when I can't even get through a stupid birthday party without going overboard. Like what's the point of the progress if it falls apart the second there's any actual pressure?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was going through your mind in the days before — when the anxiety was already building?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Just the usual stuff. What am I gonna say, how do I act normal, what if there's an awkward silence and everyone notices. And I know that sounds completely irrational but it genuinely feels like everyone is watching and waiting for me to say something dumb. The alcohol just... it turns that off. Like immediately. I feel like a different person.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It gives you relief from something that feels really overwhelming in the moment.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. And the thing is... I know it's a crutch. I've known that for a while, it's not like anyone's telling me something new. But it works. So it's hard to want to stop using something that actually helps you function, you know?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're holding two things at once — you can see that the drinking is getting in the way of where you want to be, and at the same time it's doing a real job for you right now. It's filling a gap that feels pretty essential.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... yeah. That's exactly it. And I think that's why I keep going in circles. Because I genuinely don't know what fills that gap if drinking doesn't. Like I'm not sure the version of me that doesn't drink at parties even... exists? I've never really met her.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm curious — are there situations, even smaller ones, where you've felt okay socially without needing a drink first?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um. Yeah, actually. When it's my close friends I don't really need it. Or if I have, like, a role — if I'm helping set up for something or I'm the one who knows everyone and I'm introducing people. When I'm busy I'm actually fine. It's the... standing around making small talk with people I half-know. That's the part that destroys me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there are already situations where you're navigating social stuff without relying on alcohol. You're not starting from zero — there's something there to build from.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never thought about it that way. I kind of assumed I just needed it for everything social, full stop. But... maybe it's more specific than that. Maybe it's really just the unstructured, open-ended stuff where I don't know what my role is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That feels like a meaningful thing to understand about yourself. What do you make of it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know, it's kind of... it actually makes me feel a little less hopeless about it? Like if it's not every single social situation, then maybe there's something to actually work with. I still don't know what that looks like in practice but... yeah. Maybe.

client_context: A 21-year-old college senior who binge drinks every weekend. Friends staged an intervention but the student sees it as normal college behavior.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you back. Last time we talked, things were pretty tense. How's the week been?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it's been fine. Whatever. Look, I'm only here because Dr. Reyes said I had to come back. I don't — I'm not saying I think I need to be sitting in this room again.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're here. That's what counts right now. Tell me what happened over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Nothing happened. There was a party, I drank, whatever. Everyone's acting like I committed some kind of crime. Jake — my roommate — he's been blowing up my phone like I killed someone. I blacked out, okay? It happens. It's literally college, that's what people do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you blacked out, your roommate won't leave you alone about it, and the whole thing feels wildly overblown.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... I don't actually remember the end of the night. Woke up on some random couch, my phone had like twenty missed calls. And my girlfriend — I guess ex-girlfriend now — she texted saying she's done. But that's not even about the drinking, we had other stuff going on. That's completely separate.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a lot to wake up to. What was going through your head when you saw those missed calls?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. I panicked for a second. And then I was just... mad, I guess. Because people always overreact with me. It's not like I hurt anyone. I just... I don't know what I did that night and it's... I don't know. It doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's something honest in what you just said — 'I don't know what I did.' You're not pretending that part away, and that takes something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I don't know. And I get that that's like, not ideal or whatever. But I'm not an alcoholic. My dad's an alcoholic. I grew up watching that. I know exactly what that looks like and this — this is different. I'm different.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What makes it different, in your mind?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Because I can stop when I want to. I just... choose not to on weekends because that's — because it's college. But the blackout thing... that's happened before. A few times. And I know that's probably not, like... great. But I'm still fine. I'm passing my classes, I have friends, I'm not — I'm mostly fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just try to pull this together. You woke up with no memory of the night. Your girlfriend ended things. Your roommate's scared. The blackouts have happened before — more than once. And somewhere underneath all the 'I'm fine,' there's a part of you that knows this one landed differently.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Maybe. I don't — I don't want to be my dad. That's the thing I keep coming back to. I look at him and I'm like, there's no way I'm going there. But then last weekend... I don't know what I'm doing anymore. I don't know what I want to do about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Not wanting to become your dad — that's not a small thing. That's something real in you. And right now you're sitting with not knowing what to do with it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean I'm not — I'm not ready to like quit or go to AA or whatever. But maybe I don't have to do it like this every single weekend. I don't know. Can we just... can we talk about what that would even look like? Like actually look like?

client_context: A 72-year-old with chronic pain who has been mixing alcohol with pain medication. Family is terrified. Doesn't want to burden anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thank you for coming in today. I know the court order is what brought you here, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But you also just got through detox, which is genuinely hard, and you showed up this morning. So... in your own words, what's it been like these past few weeks?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's been... I don't know. Hard. Everything still hurts — my hip, my back, same as always. And I just feel so ashamed. I never thought I'd be sitting in a place like this. Not at my age. I thought I was just... managing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you say you were managing — what did that look like for you, before all of this came to a head?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The pain is... it's constant. The doctors give me things but they don't really work, not the way I need them to. And a glass of wine at night, it just — it took the edge off. Made it so I could sleep. And then it became two glasses, and then I was mixing it with the Norco without really thinking about it, and... my daughter kept telling me something was wrong. I didn't listen. I should have listened.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the pain was real — genuinely unmanaged — and you found something that gave you some relief. And the people around you started to see it differently than you did. Your daughter was worried.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My grandson was in the car. He's eight years old. He wasn't hurt, thank God, but... he was there. And my daughter — she won't return my calls. I don't blame her. I don't blame her at all. I just... I don't see how any of this gets fixed. I'm 72 years old, I'm still in pain, and I've made a mess of everything. I don't see a way through it, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That image — your grandson in that car — you're carrying that. And I'm not going to minimize it, because it's serious and you know that. But I want to say something honest to you: you got through detox. At 72, with chronic pain that hasn't been properly treated, after all of this came crashing down — you got through it. That tells me something about who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My son drove me every single day. He took time off work. He has three kids and he took time off work for me, and I... I've spent my whole life trying not to be a burden to anybody. My husband, God rest him, he used to say I'd apologize for taking up space. And now here I am, and my children are rearranging their lives because of me. That's the part that — that's the part I can't stand.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull this together, because I want to make sure I'm understanding you. You've been living with real, undertreated pain for a long time, and you found something that helped — until it didn't. What happened with your grandson is something you think about every day. Your daughter's silence is breaking your heart. And your son showing up, as loving as that is, it sits wrong because the last thing you want is to be a weight on the people you love. And underneath all of that, there's something that wants to repair this — with your daughter, with your grandson. Am I getting that right?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's... that's exactly it. I want my daughter back. And I want — my grandson used to call me every Sunday, just to talk. About nothing, just to talk. I want that back. I want him to look at me the way he used to. That's what I want. I do want that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That matters. That's worth holding onto. What would one small step look like this week — not fixing everything, just one real thing you could actually do?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've been thinking about writing my daughter a letter. I don't know what to say exactly, I keep starting and stopping. But maybe I don't have to have it all figured out. Maybe just... that I'm sorry, and that I'm trying. Maybe that's enough to start with. I think I could do that.

client_context: An 18-year-old referred by school counselor after being caught drinking at a school event. Feels singled out since 'literally everyone drinks'.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, good to see you again. How have things been going since we last talked?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... fine, I guess. Same as always. Nothing's really changed.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fine... but something in the way you said that makes me think maybe it hasn't felt all that fine.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. I just — whatever. It's stupid. Everyone keeps making such a big deal out of everything and I'm just like... tired of it. Tired of all of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tired of all of it. And I know you mentioned the doctor's appointment when you texted — what happened there?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, so... they said some of my liver numbers were, like, off or whatever. The doctor made it sound super serious but I mean, it was probably just a fluke. My mom totally freaked out though, which made it like ten times worse.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the doctor flagged something in your results, your mom's reaction scared you — and part of you wants to believe it's nothing, even as another part of you is sitting with it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. Kind of. Like I'm not — I don't want to be the person who has liver problems at eighteen, that's just... that's not me. But also I've been drinking less, I told you that last time, so it doesn't even make sense that this is happening.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You have been cutting back — that's real work, and you did it. I want to make sure you hear that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I know, and like... I did. I really did. But then Kayla's party happened and I just — I slipped up, I guess. And then I got the results like two days later and I just felt like, what's the point, you know?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's the point... tell me more about that feeling.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like... I try, and stuff still goes wrong. And my friends are all still drinking every weekend and nobody's getting called out, nobody's getting abnormal lab results, it's just me. It feels so unfair. Like why is my body doing this when everyone else is fine?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds really lonely — doing the work, trying to change, and feeling like you're carrying something that none of your friends even have to think about.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... yeah, that's actually exactly it. It's lonely. Like I can't even talk to them about the lab stuff because they'll think I'm being dramatic. Or they'll just say 'see, one night doesn't matter.' But it does, like... I think it actually does.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me reflect back what I'm hearing — you've made real progress, you had one rough night, and then this health news hit you hard. And instead of that pushing you away from everything, part of you is saying... this is actually a sign that it matters. That your body is telling you something you can't ignore anymore.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I mean, when you say it like that. I think I always assumed I had more time — like I'm eighteen, this stuff isn't supposed to happen yet. But maybe that's kind of the point. Like, now is when it starts to actually matter.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it look like to take that seriously — in a way that actually feels like yours, not something someone is forcing on you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I actually want to go back to the doctor and ask real questions this time instead of just nodding. And maybe — maybe tell one person. Not like, announce it to everyone, just one friend I actually trust. And just go back to what I was doing before the party. Because honestly? I was doing okay.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You were doing okay. More than okay — you were doing something genuinely hard, on your own terms. One rough week doesn't erase that. It's still there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I think I needed to hear that. I keep telling myself one mistake means I failed but like... it doesn't, right? It's just one week. I can still — I can still do this.

client_context: A 34-year-old artist who believes alcohol fuels creativity. Has been drinking daily for years. Recently noticed the art has gotten worse, not better.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hi, come on in... I'm really glad you came today. I know walk-in visits can feel a little unexpected, right? Just make yourself comfortable. Can you tell me — in your own words — what brought you here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I, um... I got a call from my doctor last week. She said my labs came back and some things were... not normal. She said I should talk to someone. I don't really know what I'm doing here, honestly. I've never done anything like this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So this sort of came out of nowhere for you. Like you weren't expecting to be sitting somewhere like this, and now here you are... What was that like, getting that call?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was... scary. I mean, I knew things weren't great. I've been — I drink. I know that's probably why she sent me here. I'm not stupid. I just... I didn't think it would actually show up on a test, you know?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm. It sounds like there was a part of you that already knew, even before the test. I'm curious — what does drinking look like in your life? What role does it play for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm an artist. Like, that's how I think of myself, that's who I am. And I've always needed it — to get into that creative space, you know? I have a glass of wine and things just... open up. The ideas come. But um... lately my work hasn't been... I don't know. It's not the same.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So drinking has felt like the key that unlocks something in you — the creativity, the flow. And at the same time, you're noticing that something in the work has shifted. The art isn't coming out the way it used to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... God, it's embarrassing to say out loud. I've been telling myself it's just a block, that it'll pass. But I look at what I've made in the last year and it's... it's worse. It's genuinely worse than stuff I made ten years ago. And I don't — I don't know what to do with that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That takes real honesty, to look at your own work and let yourself see it clearly. That's not a small thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: But what if — okay, this is going to sound crazy — what if the drinking is the only thing keeping me creative at all? Like, what if I stop and there's just... nothing there? What if I was never actually talented, and the alcohol was just filling in the gaps this whole time?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're afraid that if you take away the thing you've depended on, you might find out that the art wasn't really there to begin with. That's... that's a really heavy thing to carry.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. And the thing is — I look at my work from like, five or six years ago, before things got really heavy — and it was good. It was actually good. And now it's not. So the alcohol isn't even doing what I thought it was doing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me about that time. When the art felt alive. What was that like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was... I mean, I was still drinking then, but not like this. Not every day. Not like — not from the moment I woke up or anything. I'd paint for hours and forget to eat. I'd just lose myself in it. I remember finishing pieces and feeling proud. Actually proud. I haven't felt that in a long time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you've carried this belief that the alcohol is what makes you an artist. And what you're telling me is, when you look back — the work you're most proud of, the pieces that felt alive — they came from a version of you who wasn't drinking the way you are now. That's something worth sitting with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never... I never let myself say it that way. Because if that's true, then I've been hurting the thing I love most. Trying to protect it and just... doing the opposite. This whole time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm wondering — and you don't have to have an answer right now — what would it mean to you, to get that version of yourself back? The one who could get lost in a canvas for hours?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I think I want that. I didn't know I wanted it until I heard myself say it just now. I'm scared because I don't know how to get there. But I want my art back. More than I want the other thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What I hear in everything you've shared today is someone who loves what she creates. You came in here not knowing what to expect, a little scared — and you found something real in this conversation. That honesty, that clarity about what matters to you? That's yours. And it gives us something real to work with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. I think I needed to hear myself say it out loud. I want to try. I don't know exactly what that looks like yet, but... I want to try. That's something, right?

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Come on in, Harold. Make yourself comfortable. There's no rush here — we've got plenty of time. I'm really glad you came in today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, uh... thanks. My daughter, she — she kind of insisted. I wasn't sure I'd actually walk through the door, to be honest. I've done this before, these kinds of... meetings. Didn't really go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You weren't sure you'd come in. And you've been through this before and it didn't feel like it helped. That takes something, showing up anyway.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. I don't know. My daughter means well, she does. And the doctor said some things at my last checkup that... well, they stuck with me a little. About my liver. But I mean, I'm sixty-five. Things start to go wrong, right? That's just how it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What the doctor said is sitting with you. Can you tell me a little about what's been going on for you lately — in your own words, not your daughter's, not the doctor's?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well... I retired three years ago. Thirty-two years at the same company. And I thought, you know, this is it, I earned this. But then it's just... quiet. Real quiet. My wife passed six years back, and my daughter's got her own life, kids, all of that. So it's a lot of sitting around.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thirty-two years of structure, of purpose, of knowing where you fit — and then suddenly it's gone. And you lost your wife too. That's a tremendous amount of... emptiness to sit with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's about right. Emptiness. I didn't have a word for it before but that's exactly it. I'd have a beer in the evenings with Patricia — that was my wife — just one, watching the news. Now I'm having... more than one. A fair bit more, if I'm being straight with you.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're being very honest with me, and I appreciate that. What's it like, those evenings now — without Patricia?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... God, I don't talk about this much. It's lonely. I know that sounds simple but it's a deep kind of lonely. The news comes on and I pour one, and then before I know it it's midnight and I've had... I don't even know. I just don't want to feel that quiet, you know?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The drinking fills something — it pushes back against that silence a little.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It does. For a while. And then I wake up the next morning and I feel like hell and I tell myself today's gonna be different, but then... six o'clock rolls around and the house is quiet and... it's the same thing all over again. I've been doing that cycle for about two years now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You wake up, you make yourself that promise, and then the evening comes and the pull is just too strong. And you've been carrying that cycle, mostly alone, for two years. That's exhausting, Harold.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It really is. I'm tired of it, honestly. I'm tired of waking up feeling bad. I'm tired of being... I don't know, this version of myself. Patricia would've hated seeing me like this. She was tough, she'd have said something. And that... that bothers me more than the doctor stuff, if I'm honest.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What Patricia would think — that still matters to you deeply. The man she knew, the man you were — you want to get back to something closer to him.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I do. I really do. I wasn't always like this. I coached Little League for fifteen years. I had guys I worked with, friends. I don't... I don't know where all that went. I just kind of faded out of everything when I retired.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a version of Harold who coached kids, who had people around him, who had things that gave him a reason to get up. What would it mean to you if you could find your way back toward some of that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It would mean... a lot. It would mean a lot. I've been thinking — and I haven't said this out loud to anyone — but the rec center near me does a senior softball league. I drove past the sign three times and just kept driving. But I thought about it. That's... something, right?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been driving past that sign and something in you keeps noticing it. Let me reflect back what I'm hearing today, Harold, if that's okay. You came in here not sure it would help, because it hasn't before. But you came. You talked about losing Patricia, about how retirement took away your structure and your people. You told me you're tired — tired of the cycle, tired of not being the man you want to be. And underneath all of it, there's still someone in there who coached Little League, who misses connection, who slows down at a softball sign. That person hasn't gone anywhere.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. That's — when you say it like that. I don't know, I got a little choked up there, sorry. I just haven't had anyone say it back to me like that. Most of the time I feel like I'm invisible. Just some old guy rattling around a house.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't have to apologize for that, not here. You're not invisible to me. And I'm curious — if we took just one small step, something that felt manageable, what might that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... maybe I stop in at that rec center. Just to look. And maybe I call my buddy Ray — haven't talked to him in probably eight months. I always think about it and then I don't do it. I could do that this week. Those two things feel... possible. Actually possible.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Those aren't small things, Harold. Stopping in somewhere new, picking up the phone after eight months — that's courage. You walked in here today not sure any of this would matter, and look where you are now. I'd very much like to keep talking, if you're willing to come back.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I think I will. This was... different than I expected. I'll come back.

client_context: A 72-year-old with chronic pain who has been mixing alcohol with pain medication. Family is terrified. Doesn't want to burden anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Margaret, thanks for coming in today. I know this probably wasn't your idea, so I want you to know there's no agenda here — I just want to hear how things have been going for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well... my daughter thought it would be a good idea. I've been coming to this clinic for years, so at least it's not somewhere new, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's fair — you know this place. What's your sense of why your daughter wanted you to come in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She worries too much. I've been dealing with the pain in my back for — oh, must be four years now — and I've found what helps me get through the day. She doesn't understand that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So from your side, you've figured out what works, and she's worried about something she doesn't fully understand.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. I mean... yes. The doctor gives me those pills and they — they help, but not all the way, you know? And a glass of wine in the evening takes the edge off. I'm not hurting anybody.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about the pain itself — what does a bad day actually look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh... it's constant. It never fully goes away. Some mornings I can barely get out of bed. The medication helps for maybe a few hours, and then... and then I just need something. I know mixing them isn't exactly what the doctor ordered, but what am I supposed to do — just suffer?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been managing something really difficult, mostly on your own, for a long time. And it sounds like you've been doing whatever you can to not ask for more help.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want to be a burden. My kids have their own lives. They've got grandchildren, they've got jobs... I'm not going to call my daughter every time my back hurts.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And yet she's here. She came with you today. What do you think that tells you about how she sees this situation?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She's scared. I can see it on her face... She found me asleep on the couch and couldn't wake me for a bit. She thought — well. She thought something had happened to me. And I... I didn't realize it looked like that to her.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying all this pain quietly — trying to protect her — and she's been terrified anyway. That's a hard thing to sit with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never thought about it that way... I thought I was doing the right thing. Staying out of her hair. Not making her feel like she has to take care of me. But maybe I... maybe I got that wrong.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would being a good mother — or grandmother — actually look like to you, if you could picture it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Being... present, I suppose. At the holidays. Seeing my granddaughter grow up. I want to be there for that. I really do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That matters to you deeply — I can hear that. And I want to be straight with you, because I think you can handle it: mixing pain medication with alcohol, even small amounts, is genuinely dangerous at your dosage. I'm not saying that to frighten you. I'm saying it because you just told me the people you love most are scared of losing you, and I think you deserve to know the full picture.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I know. I think... part of me has known for a while. I just didn't want to admit that I needed help. I'm 72 years old — I thought I was past all this sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing. You've been in real pain for years, you've been managing it alone because you didn't want to be a burden, and somewhere along the way it started to frighten the people who love you most. And today, sitting here, you're starting to wonder if there might be a safer path — one that still lets you be present for your granddaughter. That kind of honesty with yourself takes real strength.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It does... it doesn't come easy to me, asking for help. But maybe it's time. I'd like to — I'd like to at least talk to someone about the pain management. See if there's something safer I can do. My daughter would be so relieved.

client_context: A 50-year-old who was sober for 3 years but relapsed after a sudden job loss. Feels deep shame and hopelessness. Has been to AA before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know starting over with someone new isn't always easy, especially if you've been through this before. What would be most useful for you to talk about?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh... I'm not really sure, honestly. My doctor referred me. Said I should come in. So. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Here you are. Tell me a bit about what's been going on — in your own words, no rush.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I, uh... I lost my job. Back in January. Twenty-two years at the same place and they just — let me go. And I... I started drinking again after that. Three years sober and I just... [exhales] yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Three years. And then everything shifted at once — the job, the ground under your feet — and the drinking came back.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I know the whole drill, okay? I've done AA. I've sat in rooms like this. Talked to people. And I still... [long pause] I don't even know why I'm here, no offense. Nothing's ever stuck. So I'm not sure what's gonna be different this time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Three years is real. That didn't vanish — it happened, and you built it. What was actually working back then, when things were holding together?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I had... structure, I guess. The job gave me somewhere to be every morning. My wife and I were in a better place. And I had a sponsor I actually trusted — like, really trusted. When all of that kind of collapsed at once... I didn't even fight it. Honestly. I just didn't have anything left to hold onto.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me make sure I'm getting this right. You know how to get sober — you've done it. What held you there was real stuff: work, your marriage being steadier, a sponsor you could be honest with. And when those things fell away at the same time, the drinking wasn't really a decision. It was more like the floor giving out.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Yeah, that's — I never actually put it like that before. [pause] I always just figured I was weak. That I gave up. But it wasn't like I wanted to drink. I just... had nothing to stand on. [quieter] I don't know if I can do three years again. But maybe I don't have to think about it that way.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just said something important — you don't have to think about three years. So what would feel like a real place to start, for you, right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Getting through today without feeling like a complete failure would be something. [small laugh] And... finding somebody I can actually talk to. Not worksheets. I want to understand what happened this time — like really understand it — so I'm not sitting in another one of these chairs five years from now saying the same thing.

client_context: A 40-year-old single parent who has been drinking a bottle of wine nightly to cope with the stress of raising two kids alone. Knows it's too much but feels trapped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for making time for this today — I know doing it over video from home can feel a little strange. I want this to be your space, really. So... what's on your mind? What feels most important to bring into the room today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... honestly I wasn't sure about coming. The school counselor kind of — she sort of pushed me into it. I don't think I really have a, like... I'm fine. I'm just stressed. Every parent is stressed, right?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're fine. And also — really stressed. Those two things can both be true at the same time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean... it is what it is. I'm a single mom, I've been doing this alone for four years. The stress is just — that's just life. I'm not falling apart or anything. I still get them to school, I still go to work. I'm handling it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Four years of doing this by yourself. That's a long time to be the only one holding everything together. I'm curious — what does a typical evening look like for you, once the kids are down?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I pour a glass of wine. Maybe more than one glass. It's like — it's the only part of the day that's mine, you know? The house finally gets quiet and I can just... breathe. Stop being 'Mom' for five minutes. Is that so terrible?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound terrible at all. It sounds like those quiet moments with a glass of wine are the only time in your entire day when you get to just... exist as a person. Not as somebody's mom, not as somebody's employee. Just you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. [pause] Yeah, that's — that's exactly it. [quieter] I've been going through a bottle most nights, if I'm being honest. I know that's a lot. I know. But it doesn't feel like a choice anymore, it just feels like... the only way to make it to morning.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What you just said — that took real honesty. And I just want to sit with that for a second, because I think you're describing something that a lot of people never even let themselves name out loud. You are carrying something enormous. Alone. Every single day.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My daughter said something last week. She said — [voice catches] — she goes, 'Mommy, you smell like juice at night.' She's seven. She said it totally matter-of-fact, like it was just a thing. And I laughed it off in the moment but I haven't stopped thinking about it. Like... three days I've been sitting with that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment is still with you. [pause] She noticed. And you noticed that she noticed. [long pause] When you let yourself imagine things looking even a little bit different... what do you picture?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I want to actually be there at bedtime. Not just like, physically in the room going through the motions. Actually there. Sometimes I tuck them in and by the time I walk out I can't remember what we even talked about. I don't want that. I don't want to miss it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You want to remember. You want to be present — really present — not just in the room.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [quietly] Yeah, I do. I think I convinced myself the wine was helping — like, at least I wasn't yelling at them, at least I was calmer. But I'm starting to think... maybe I'm just... not there either way. Just in a different way.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to reflect something back, because I think you said something really important tonight. You came in not sure why you were here. And somewhere in this conversation, you named what actually matters to you — being truly present for your kids, not just surviving until the next morning. You named that the wine started as something that was yours, something that helped you breathe, but that it's gotten to a place where it doesn't feel like a choice. And that moment with your daughter — you're still carrying it. That's not someone who doesn't care. That's someone who cares deeply. I'm wondering — is there one small thing you might want to just notice this week? Not change, just... notice.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... yeah. Just noticing when I reach for it. Asking myself if I actually need it right now or if I'm just — on autopilot. I think I can do that. Maybe that's a place to start.

client_context: A 26-year-old software engineer with severe social anxiety who uses alcohol as liquid courage at every social event. Knows it's a crutch but terrified of life without it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, welcome back. Good to see you. How are things going since we last met?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... okay, I guess? I mean, it's been kind of a rough week, honestly. I almost didn't come in today, I was like — I don't know, I didn't really want to have to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about what made it rough.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: There was a work happy hour on Friday and I... I had way more than I was supposed to. Like, significantly more. And the thing is — I could feel it coming. Like, I knew before I even walked in that it was going to happen, and I still just... did it anyway. So that was fun.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you was watching it happen in almost real time — and it happened anyway.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly like that. Which is honestly kind of terrifying, right? Like knowing and still doing it. I don't know what that says about me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to push back on that a little — the fact that you could name what was happening even in the moment? That's actually not nothing. That's a part of you paying attention. What was going on for you leading up to the happy hour?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, happy hours are like... they're my worst nightmare. No agenda, just standing around making small talk with people I see every day but don't actually know. I can sit alone and write code for eight hours no problem, but put me in a circle with drinks and I just — freeze. Like, completely. Unless I have a drink first.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does it actually feel like right before you take that first drink at something like that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like... my chest gets really tight. And I can feel everyone looking at me even when they're definitely not. And I'm already running through like, exit strategies — how do I leave without it being weird, do I fake a phone call, whatever. The drink just makes it stop. Immediately. It's not even about getting drunk, it's just... off switch. That's literally all it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's the only off switch that actually works.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've tried other stuff. The breathing, the grounding thing, the whole — whatever. But in the moment? Standing there with everyone around? They don't work. Or I don't trust them, maybe. I'm not sure which. It feels kind of stupid to even admit that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound stupid — it sounds like you haven't found anything that feels as fast or as guaranteed. That's actually a really meaningful distinction. So let me ask you something kind of weird: what would it even look like for you to be at a work thing and just... feel okay? Without the drink?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... huh. I don't think I've actually thought about it that way. Like, what does okay even feel like for me in that situation? I'm not sure I know. Maybe just... not wanting to leave every five minutes? Not feeling like I'm performing being a normal person?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just described a version of yourself you haven't fully met yet. Someone who can actually be present without running an escape route in the background the whole time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: God. When you put it like that it's kind of... sad? Like I've been showing up to my own life with a crutch for so long I genuinely don't know if I can walk without it. That's a weird thing to realize sitting in this office on a Thursday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to reflect back what I'm hearing, because there's actually a lot happening here. You came in today not wanting to talk about a rough week. You told me about Friday — how you could see it coming and felt kind of stuck anyway. You described the anxiety as this chest-tight, everybody's-watching thing that alcohol turns off faster than anything else. And now you're sitting here wondering whether there's a version of you on the other side of this who can actually just... be there. That's a lot of layers to be holding.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it is. I always kind of framed it as like, 'I drink because I'm anxious,' but... it's more like I never actually learned to be anxious and just survive it? Like, I always had the exit. That feels different from what I thought.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Underneath all of this — the court stuff, the happy hours, the off switch — what matters most to you about actually figuring this out?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? The court thing is annoying but that's not really... that's not it. I think I just want to stop being scared of my own coworkers. Which sounds so dumb when I say it out loud but it's true. I want to actually be at things. Not just physically present, like — actually there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That wanting — to actually be there, not just show up — that sounds like it comes from somewhere pretty real.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It does. I think underneath all of it I actually want real connection. Like, actual stuff with people. And I've been using the exact thing that makes me seem okay on the outside while completely blocking me from getting there. That's... kind of a mindf*** honestly. Sorry — is that okay to say?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Ha — yes, that's okay to say. And also — you just named something really important. The thing you're using to get close to people might be the exact thing holding you at arm's length from them. You've done some genuinely honest work today, especially after a week you didn't even want to talk about. So where do you want to go from here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I want to actually try the anxiety work for real. Not just in my apartment doing breathing exercises by myself. Like... maybe actually tell my therapist it's gotten worse than I've let on, or look into — I don't know, exposure therapy or something. I'm not saying I'm ready to walk into a happy hour sober next week. But maybe I can start smaller than that.

client_context: A 72-year-old with chronic pain who has been mixing alcohol with pain medication. Family is terrified. Doesn't want to burden anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back. I'm glad. Last time felt a little rough toward the end — how have you been this week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I almost didn't. Honestly. But... I don't know. I kept thinking about what you said. So here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me what your week looked like. Day to day.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Same as always, really. The mornings aren't so bad. I take my pills, have my tea, watch the birds out the back window. But afternoons... the pain gets worse, and I might have a glass or two of wine. I've been doing that for years. It helps.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The wine has been your way of getting through the hard part of the day.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well... yes. But then the doctor — she called me in about those lab results, and she had this look on her face. I don't... I'm 72. My body isn't going to be perfect. But she said something about my liver and I've been... I can't stop thinking about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Those results scared you. What was going through your mind when she said that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That I didn't want my children to find out. That's — that's the first thing I thought. Not even about me, really. My daughter already calls twice a week checking in. If she knew how much I've been drinking on top of the medication, she'd — she'd want to take over. Move me somewhere. And I can't have that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're protecting them — and protecting your independence at the same time. And underneath all of that, there's real fear about what these results might mean.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want to be a burden. Harold — my husband — he was sick for three years before he passed. I watched what that did to everyone. I won't put my kids through that. I won't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You watched your family carry something very heavy, and you made a quiet promise to yourself that you wouldn't do that to them. That says a lot about who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: But I'm not... I mean, wine isn't the same as being sick, is it? It's just something I do. It's not like I'm — I'm not an alcoholic or anything like that. I just... some days it's the only thing that makes the afternoon bearable.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I hear you — you're not saying there's a big problem. And at the same time, you're telling me those afternoons are very hard to get through, and the lab results are giving you pause. Both of those things can be true at once.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I suppose they can. I haven't really let myself think about it that way. You just — when you're in pain every day, you find what gets you through and you hold on to it. You don't stop to ask too many questions.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Can I be direct with you about something? The combination of alcohol and the pain medications you're on — it's hard on the liver in a specific way. Your numbers are already showing that effect. I'm not saying this to frighten you. I'm saying it because you strike me as someone who wants the honest picture.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yes. Yes, I do. I've been telling myself it's fine, but... I think I've known for a while something wasn't right. My stomach's been off. I haven't slept well. I just kept... not looking at it directly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing from you today. You came back — and that took something. You're not drinking to escape, you're drinking to survive real pain and real loneliness in those long afternoons. The thing that frightens you most isn't your health — it's becoming a burden to the people you love. And now something in you is saying: maybe this path leads exactly where I don't want to go.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... yes. That's exactly it. When you say it like that. I don't want to end up helpless because I was too stubborn to deal with this. Harold would have told me to be practical. He was always the practical one. So — what can I actually do? Is there something for the pain that isn't... that wouldn't do this to me?

utterances.speaker: therapist
