utterances.text: There are real options — on the pain side, working with your doctor to look at what else might help, and on the afternoons, figuring out what else could be in that space with you. We don't have to solve everything today. What feels like one thing you could do before we meet again?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I need to be honest with Dr. Reeves. Tell her how much I've actually been drinking. I've been... not exactly lying, but I haven't given her the full picture. I think I can do that. I think I'm ready to do that.

client_context: A 50-year-old who was sober for 3 years but relapsed after a sudden job loss. Feels deep shame and hopelessness. Has been to AA before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm Dave — most people skip the 'Dr. Martinez' thing after about thirty seconds. I know you probably weren't planning on this being how your day went. How're you holding up?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm... fine. I mean, not fine, obviously. If I was fine I wouldn't be sitting here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fair enough. The ER isn't exactly where most people put on their calendar. What happened, from your side of things?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I, uh... I had a lot to drink. Too much. My neighbor called 911, I guess. I don't really remember much after like nine o'clock. Woke up with an IV in my arm and some kid in scrubs asking me if I knew what year it was.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Sounds like that was a pretty rough way to come back to earth.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's embarrassing. That's what it is. I was sober for three years. Three. Years. And I just... I threw it all away. Just like that. What kind of person does that?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Three years is not a small thing. That's three years of showing up every day and doing the hard work. That doesn't disappear.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. Look how it turned out.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something had to have shifted. What was going on in your life around the time things started to unravel?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Lost my job. Six weeks ago. Twenty-two years at the same company and then just... boom. 'Position eliminated.' Box of stuff on your desk by noon. I don't... I don't even know what I'm supposed to do now. I'm fifty years old. Who the hell is gonna hire me?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Twenty-two years and then the floor just drops out from under you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's exactly what it felt like. Like... I didn't even know who I was without that job. I'd wake up in the morning and there was just — nothing. Nowhere to be. And I kept thinking, I'll get back on my feet, I'll figure it out, but the days just kept going by and I wasn't figuring anything out and then one night I just... I bought a bottle.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like structure was doing a lot of heavy lifting for your recovery — maybe more than you realized. When you were solid those three years, what else was keeping you on track besides work?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: AA. I was going three times a week. Had a sponsor, Frank, good guy. He still calls me actually. I just... I haven't picked up. I don't know what to say to him. I feel like I let him down too, on top of everything else.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: He's still calling. That says something — about him, yeah, but also about what you two built together. It sounds like part of what's crushing you right now isn't just the relapse, it's that you lost the whole scaffolding at once. The job, the routine, the meetings — all of it at the same time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never... huh. I never really thought about it that way. I just thought I was weak. That I couldn't handle things like a normal person. But when you put it like that... I mean, a lot did come apart at once, didn't it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If you did pick up when Frank calls — and I'm not saying you have to, just imagining it — what do you think you'd want him to know?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That I messed up. That I'm ashamed. That I... I don't know. That I'm scared. I'm scared this is just who I am. That I'm always gonna be the guy who caves when things get hard.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're worried this slip is a verdict. Like it means something final about who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... I know it doesn't have to be. I've been through the steps. I know relapse isn't the end, I've sat in rooms where guys have relapsed five, six times and come back. I know all of that. But knowing something up here and actually feeling it are two completely different things.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, make sure I've got it right. You've got three years of real recovery behind you — AA, a sponsor, the steps, the whole thing. You know how it works, you've done it. Then six weeks ago you lost something enormous, and it pulled the rug out from under the whole structure that was holding you together. You didn't pick up because things were fine — you picked up because you were drowning. And now here you are, sitting in this room, which — and I want to name this — you almost certainly didn't have to do. You could've just walked out of that ER and gone home.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I almost didn't come. I sat in the parking lot for like twenty minutes. I thought about just leaving.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: But you didn't. So — what does the part of you that walked through that door want to do with this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I need to call Frank back. I know I need to do that. And I need to get back to meetings, I think. I don't know what to do about the job stuff yet, that's still — that's still a lot. But I can't keep doing this. I can't wake up not knowing if I'm gonna make it through the day. I did it before. I know I did it before.

client_context: A 72-year-old with chronic pain who has been mixing alcohol with pain medication. Family is terrified. Doesn't want to burden anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Come on in, please. I know you mentioned at the front desk you're a little pressed for time today, and I really appreciate you being here anyway. That matters. So... what's going on for you right now? What made you come in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well... my friend Patricia, she — she sort of made me. I mean, she didn't drag me here, but she sat me down last week and she was crying and I just... I couldn't say no to her. She's known me forty years. I told her I was fine, I told everyone I was fine, but she wouldn't — she just kept saying she was scared. And I thought, well, I can at least come talk to somebody. I'm not sure what I'm supposed to say.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Patricia loves you. And you love her enough that her fear moved you. Even when you didn't fully agree with her... you still showed up. That says a lot about who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Mm. I suppose. I've always been the one people lean on, not the other way around. My late husband, my kids when they were young — I just, that's how it's always been. You take care of things. You don't make a fuss. The pain's been bad lately, that's really all it is. The doctor gave me something for it, Norco, and sometimes at night when it's really bad I'll have a glass of wine to... help it along. That's not — that's not the same as having a problem, is it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've spent a lifetime holding things together for everyone else. And now the pain is bad enough that you're reaching for anything that gives you some relief. I'm curious... what does nighttime look like for you? When it gets to that point where you need the wine on top of the medication.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... the quiet is hard. My hip, the arthritis — it gets loud at night, if that makes any sense. And I lie there and I think, I can't call my daughter at two in the morning, she has work, she has her own children. I can't be that person. So I take the pill, and then maybe an hour later I think, well, it's still not enough, and I have the wine. Just the one glass. Sometimes two. And I go to sleep. That's all. But Patricia saw the bottles and she — she counted them, apparently. I didn't know she was counting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She counted them because she was frightened... and somewhere in you, you knew why she was frightened. Or you wouldn't be here. You'd have stayed home.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I know mixing them is... I'm not stupid, I'm a grown woman, I know what I'm doing. But I thought — I thought I was being careful. I thought it was just enough to get through the night without calling anyone. Without being a burden. And now Patricia's frightened and my daughter called me twice this week and I can hear it in her voice and I just... I don't want to be the thing everyone worries about. I really don't. I've never wanted that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been trying so hard to protect everyone from your pain... and it's turned into something that now scares the people who love you most. That's an incredibly lonely place to be carrying by yourself. What would it mean for you — just for you — if the nights got a little easier without having to rely on the wine?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I think I could sleep. Actually sleep, not just go under. And maybe I'd stop dreading going to bed, I don't know. There's part of me that knows I've been — I've been sliding. I can feel it. I just didn't want to say it out loud. Patricia was the first person brave enough to say it to me and I was so angry at her. And then I just... I cried for about an hour after she left.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think you've said some really important things. You came in today because someone who loves you was scared — and because part of you recognized she wasn't wrong. You've been in real pain, physical pain that nobody should have to manage alone in the middle of the night, and you've been using whatever was available to get through it without asking for help. Not because you don't matter, but because you've spent your whole life making sure you don't take up too much space. And somewhere this week... that started to feel like it wasn't working anymore. Does that feel right to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. That's — yeah. That's exactly right. I didn't think anyone would put it like that. I thought you'd tell me I had a drinking problem and give me a pamphlet. ... Can I come back? Even if I'm — I know I'm rushed today, but can I come back and maybe actually talk about what to do about the nights?

client_context: A 37-year-old middle school teacher who drinks every evening and occasionally comes to work hungover. A colleague noticed and expressed concern privately.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's really good to see you again. Come on in, make yourself comfortable. So... how have things been since we last talked? I know you mentioned last time you were starting to find a bit of a groove.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, um... okay, I guess. I mean, it was going... it was going okay for a while there. And then, I don't know, this week kind of fell apart a little bit. So. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So something shifted this week. It sounds like there was a stretch where things were moving in the right direction, and then something happened that made it harder.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I had cut back, like, I was doing pretty well. I think I had maybe three or four nights where I just had one or two and then stopped. Which is — I know that probably doesn't sound like much but for me that was... that was different. And then, I don't know, Tuesday night just kind of went sideways.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Four nights of doing something different — that actually is a lot. I want to hear more about Tuesday. What was going on for you that evening?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: We had this... okay so there's this parent, right, whose kid has been a nightmare all semester — and I feel terrible saying that about a twelve-year-old but it's true — and she sent this email to the principal basically implying I have a drinking problem. To my principal. I don't even know how she... I mean, maybe someone talked, I don't know. I just — I got home and I was shaking and I just, I opened a bottle and I didn't really stop until I went to bed.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds terrifying. Someone going to your principal... that's your livelihood, your reputation — everything you've worked for. And in that moment, when you were shaking and scared, the drink was the thing that felt like it could take the edge off.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's not like I'm — look, I've been teaching for eleven years. Eleven years. I have never, not once, been impaired in front of my students. I would never do that. This parent doesn't know what she's talking about. The email was completely out of line and the principal basically said so.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your commitment to those kids — eleven years — that's real. That matters to you enormously. And I hear you that you felt deeply misrepresented. I'm also noticing... you came back here today. Even after a week like that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I almost didn't. I was sitting in the parking lot for like fifteen minutes. I kept thinking, this is embarrassing, what am I even doing here, I don't — I don't have a problem like the people who actually need this. I just drink to unwind. Everyone does.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm. Part of you is still not sure you belong here. And another part of you sat in that parking lot for fifteen minutes and then walked through the door anyway.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I guess so. I don't know. I just — the Tuesday thing scared me a little. Not the email. I mean, that scared me too. But more like... how fast I went from feeling okay, like actually okay for a few days, and then one bad night and it was like those four days never happened.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does it mean to you that it happened that quickly?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I think it means I've been telling myself a story. Like, that I'm the one who's in charge of it. That I do it because I choose to and I can choose not to whenever I want. And Tuesday kind of... poked a hole in that. Because I didn't really feel like I chose anything. I just did it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took real honesty to say. The gap between the story we tell ourselves and what we actually notice happening — sitting with that is uncomfortable. And you're sitting with it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's just... I love my job. I actually love it. Those kids drive me crazy but I genuinely love being in that classroom. And I — I can't lose that. I can't have it be the thing that... I don't want to be the teacher who lost everything because of this. That's not who I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That classroom, those kids — that's at the center of who you are. And I'm hearing you say very clearly: you don't want this to take that from you. What would it look like, do you think, to protect that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... probably actually doing what I was doing those four days. Not just cutting back but having something I do instead of just sitting alone with a bottle. My wife suggested I start going to the gym after school instead of coming straight home but I kind of blew that off. Maybe that was dumb.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your wife offered that to you — and you're considering it now, even if you weren't ready then. That gap between school and home sounds like it carries a lot of weight. Like something happens in that transition.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. That's — that's exactly it, actually. It's like the second I walk in the door and it's quiet, everything from the day just lands on me. And the drink is the thing that... softens it, I guess. But maybe the gym could do that. I haven't really let myself think about it that way.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're seeing a different possibility there — something that could soften the landing without costing you what you're afraid of losing. What feels like the smallest possible step you could take before we meet again?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I could just... try the gym thing once. One afternoon. See how it feels. I'm not promising anything, I'm just — yeah. One time. That I can probably do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just take a moment to hold what you've shared today. You came in after a really hard week — a week where a parent's email rattled you down to your foundation, and Tuesday night was tough. And underneath all of that, you noticed something honest: that the control you thought you had felt different in the moment. You named what matters most to you — that classroom, those kids, your marriage. And you left yourself one small, concrete thing to try. That's not nothing. That's actually quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. When you put it like that. I don't know, I came in here feeling like I'd just blown everything and I don't feel like that right now. Which is weird. I'll, um. I'll try the gym thing. And I'll come back.

client_context: A 33-year-old social media influencer whose entire social life revolves around drinking. Multiple friends have expressed concern. Insists it's just her lifestyle.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know this isn't exactly how you planned to spend your Friday. Before we get into anything formal — how are you doing right now, coming out of the detox program?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... honestly? I'm fine. Like, better than fine — I feel great, actually. Everyone keeps acting like I was on death's door or something, but I just needed a reset, you know? It's not a big deal. I've done cleanses before. This was just a more... medical one.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A reset. Something that feels familiar to you, manageable — not really in the same category as what the people around you seem to be treating it as.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. See, you get it. My followers do a juice cleanse and it's like, inspirational content. I do a supervised detox and suddenly everyone's staging intervention meetings and calling my mom and... [waves hand] It's honestly a little ironic, right? [laughs softly] I mean, I'm the most self-aware person in most rooms I walk into. I know myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you make of the fact that multiple people in your life — and then the courts — ended up concerned enough to get you here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay, the court thing is — look, I was at a rooftop event, I made a bad call getting behind the wheel, and I fully own that part. That was wrong, I'm not defending it. But one bad decision doesn't mean I have a drinking problem. Plenty of people make that mistake once. I just happened to have visibility, so it became this whole... situation. My publicist had to issue a statement. Do you know how humiliating that is? I had brands reaching out to pause partnerships.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Taking responsibility for that night — that does take something. And I'm also noticing that underneath the logistics of all this, there's real embarrassment. Not just inconvenience.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. It wasn't my best look. [quieter] Not even close. But I have a brand, you know? Everything I've built — my whole audience trusts me to be authentic with them, and I am, I really am, just... not about this. Not yet. This isn't the kind of story I'm ready to tell. I'm still figuring out what the story even is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you say 'not yet' and 'not ready' — I'm curious what you imagine would have to be different for you to feel ready.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... hm. [pause] That's actually kind of a weird question. I don't know. I guess if it was actually a real problem? Like, if things were falling apart in some concrete way. But my content is performing well, my engagement is up, I'm showing up to things... I'm functional. [quieter, almost to herself] Most days.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Most days.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... [longer pause] I mean, there are mornings that are... harder than others. And my best friend Kayla — she's been kind of distant since everything happened, and that actually really hurts. We used to go out together all the time and now she won't really return my calls. I don't know if that's about me, or the incident, or the drinking, or — [looks down] It's probably all of it. It's probably all of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Underneath all the noise of the brand and the court stuff and the publicist — there are relationships that matter deeply to you. And you're starting to wonder, out loud, whether drinking is getting in the way of those.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want to lose Kayla. Like, genuinely. And my mom — [trails off, swallows] she cried when I got out of the detox facility. She never cries, she's not that kind of person. And I kept saying 'Mom, I'm fine, I'm fine,' and she just held my face and said 'I know you think you are.' [pause] I've been thinking about that a lot. I have been. I still don't think I'm an alcoholic — that word doesn't feel like me at all — but... maybe something is off. Maybe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I've heard from you today. You came in saying this was a reset — a cleanse, manageable, not a big deal. And in the same conversation, you talked about mornings that are hard, Kayla going quiet, your mom crying at the door of the facility, and a feeling that maybe something is off. You're not ready to use certain words, and you're here asking real questions. That's not nothing. That's actually the beginning of something important.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [soft, slightly surprised laugh] I came in here fully prepared to charm my way through this session, if I'm being honest. Like I had a whole... vibe planned. [pause] But I don't know. Maybe I can actually use this. I'm not making any promises. I'm not signing anything. But I think I might be willing to keep talking.

client_context: A 55-year-old who lost their spouse 8 months ago and has been drinking to numb the pain. Isolated from friends and family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today, Margaret. I know this might not be... entirely your choice, given the circumstances. I want you to know there's no agenda here — I'm not here to tell you what to do or judge anything you share. Mostly I just want to understand a bit about where things are at for you. Does that sound okay?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Sure. Fine. I've done this before, you know — the counseling thing. A few times actually. So... yeah. I'm here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been through this process before, and here you are again. What would you want me to understand about what's brought you in this time — in your own words?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My employer sent me. There was an... incident. At work. I'd had a couple drinks at lunch and apparently that's a fireable offense now, which — look, I've been doing that job for eleven years without a single complaint, so. It was one time. They're making it into something it isn't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Eleven years of solid work, and this one thing has suddenly put all of that at risk. That feels deeply unfair.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It... yes. It does. I mean, I know how it looks. I'm not an idiot. But I wasn't — I wasn't drunk, I just had a glass of wine with lunch, maybe two, because it had been a really hard morning and I just needed to... take the edge off a little. I went right back to my desk. It's not like I was falling down or something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like mornings can be really hard right now. I don't want to skip over that. Can you tell me a little about what's been going on in your life over... I don't know, the past year or so?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My husband passed. Eight months ago. Heart attack. He was... we were married thirty-one years. So. That's been — yeah, that's been a lot to deal with. The kids have their own lives, they live out of state, and I just... I've been managing on my own.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thirty-one years. And then suddenly you're navigating all of it — the grief, the empty house, the day-to-day — completely alone. That's an enormous weight to carry.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I... yeah. I won't lie, the drinking has gotten — it's more than it used to be. Since he died. I know that. I'm not going to sit here and pretend otherwise. Evenings especially. The house is just so quiet and I don't really know what to do with myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I appreciate you saying that — it takes something to name it out loud. When you pour that drink in the evening, what does it give you in that moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It... it quiets things. The thoughts, the — I keep thinking about things I should have said to him, things I should have done differently. And the wine just... turns the volume down. For a little while. But then I wake up at three in the morning and it's all right there again, so. I don't know. Maybe it's not actually helping as much as I think it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really honest observation — that part of you is starting to question whether it's actually doing what you need it to do. You're carrying this grief and you found something that gives you a few hours of relief, and at the same time you're noticing there's a cost.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The mornings are awful. I feel terrible, I feel... ashamed, kind of. Which is a word I never thought I'd use about myself. I used to be — I ran the PTA, I organized fundraisers, I was the person people called when they needed help. And now I'm... this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That woman you're describing — the one people called, the one who showed up — she's still in there, Margaret. What would it mean to you to find your way back to something closer to her?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... god. I'm sorry. I didn't — I don't usually cry in these things. I just... I miss him so much. And I think I've been so busy trying not to feel it that I haven't actually... I don't know what I'd even be going back to. But I don't want to keep living like this. I really don't. This isn't — this isn't what he would have wanted for me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Please don't apologize. What I'm hearing is someone who has been through an incredible loss, who's been trying to survive it the best way she knew how, and who — today, right now — is recognizing that the way she's been coping is starting to cost her the things she actually values: her work, her sense of herself, maybe even the way she wants to honor her husband. That's not a small thing to sit with. That takes real courage to say out loud.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've never thought about it that way. Like — honoring him. He would have hated seeing me like this. He always said I was the strong one. I want to... I think I actually want to try. For the first time in a long time, I think I mean that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I believe you. Given everything you've just shared, what feels like it might be one small thing — doesn't have to be big — that could be a first step toward that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... I used to go to a grief support group at my church. I stopped because it felt like too much, too many people, but... maybe I could try that again. And coming back here. I think I'd like to come back here, if that's — yeah. I think that might actually help.

client_context: A 48-year-old who has been drinking heavily since his divorce 4 months ago. Alternates between anger at his ex and sadness about losing his family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I'm Marcus, one of the counselors here on walk-in days. These sessions are a little different than a scheduled appointment — there's no set agenda, really. Just whatever's on your mind. So... what brought you in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, uh... honestly I wasn't sure I was even gonna come in. Sat in my car for like fifteen minutes out there. My doctor mentioned this place after my last checkup and I figured... I don't know. Something's gotta give, right? It's just been a rough few months. Real rough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something's gotta give — that's a pretty significant thing to say. What's been going on these past few months?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My wife left. Ex-wife now, I guess. Four months ago. Twenty-two years and she just... anyway. I've been drinking more than I probably should, I'll admit that. My buddy noticed, my doctor noticed. I notice. But it's not like — I mean, divorce is rough. That's not unusual, right? To drink a little more when your whole life falls apart? I still go to work, I pay my bills, I have my kids every other weekend. I function.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So on one hand, you can see that the drinking has gone up, and the people close to you are noticing. And on the other hand, it feels like a pretty understandable response to something as brutal as a divorce — especially after twenty-two years.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. I'm not some — I'm not sitting in a ditch, okay? I just... the nights are bad. I won't lie. After the kids go to bed, or when I'm in that apartment alone, I pour a drink, then another, and suddenly it's two in the morning and I'm just sitting there furious at her all over again. Going over everything she said. What she did. And I can't — I can't turn it off. So yeah. I drink. And I know how that sounds.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You showed up here today — that takes something. And listening to you, it's clear you're a man who cares a lot. About your kids, about keeping it together, about not becoming someone you don't recognize. That matters.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't feel like I'm keeping it together. Not really. My youngest — she's fourteen — she asked me last week if I was okay. Fourteen years old. She's dealing with her parents splitting up and she's checking on me. That's... that hit different. That's kind of the real reason I'm here, actually. That moment right there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment with your daughter sounds like it cut right through everything. What was that like for you — hearing her ask that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like I failed. Like she shouldn't have to worry about me — she's a kid. And I just said 'I'm fine, sweetheart' and I wasn't. I'm not. And I know the drinking isn't helping, I know that, I just... I don't know what else to do with it. The anger, the... I miss my family. I miss waking up in my own house. I miss it being normal. I just miss my life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Underneath all that anger at her — there's a lot of grief there. Missing your life. Missing what was normal. And maybe the drinking has been the only thing you've found that gets you through the nights when all of that is just... too much to sit with alone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... I think that's right. I tell myself I'm angry because anger you can do something with, you know? Angry feels like you're still fighting. Sad is just... sad. And I've been carrying a lot of sad. I just haven't let myself. ... I don't really know how to do that.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, good to see you back. Honestly? I wasn't totally sure you'd show. That takes something — coming back when you didn't exactly sign up for this in the first place.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah well. HR made it pretty clear it wasn't optional so... here I am. Again.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Right, the incident. Look, I'm not here to go back over the report — I've read it. What I'm actually curious about is what was going on for you that day. Like, in your head, before any of it happened.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What was going on? Nothing. I had a couple drinks at lunch, it's not — guys in my unit used to do a lot worse before a patrol and nobody wrote anybody up for that. This whole thing is a different standard and honestly it's... it's bullshit. I function fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So what got you through over there — what kept you standing — doesn't exactly fly back here, and now you're being judged by rules that feel like they don't account for any of that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I mean — yeah. Over there nobody cared how you coped as long as you showed up. You survived, you drank, you did it again the next day. That was just — that was the culture. And now I'm supposed to fit into some cubicle and act like none of it happened? I don't even know what that looks like.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's real — carrying all of that and then being expected to just switch it off like a light. I want to ask you something, and you can tell me to go to hell if you want. Last time you mentioned your wife said something about where things stand between you two. Where's that at now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She, um... she said she's done. Those were her exact words. Done. And I keep telling myself I'm not some — I'm not a drunk, okay? I go to work, I pay the mortgage, I show up. But she's... I don't know. Maybe she's seeing something I'm not seeing. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That landed different than the work stuff, didn't it. 'Maybe she's seeing something I'm not' — man, that's not a small thing to say out loud.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want to lose my family. The job — I could find another job, whatever. But my daughter is seven. She asked my wife last week why daddy smells funny when he picks her up from school and I just... that's not — that's not who I want to be. That's not the dad I said I was gonna be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think it matters. You came back from deployment carrying something heavy, and drinking was how you and everyone around you stayed afloat over there — that part makes complete sense given what you lived through. Coming home, the rules changed but nobody handed you a different playbook. And now you're here, and the thing that actually cuts through all of it — not HR, not your boss — it's your daughter asking that question. That tells me something about what you're actually fighting for.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm not — I'm still not putting a label on it, I'm not ready for that. But yeah. Something's gotta change. I just... I don't know where you even start with something like this.

client_context: A 42-year-old construction worker who drinks a six-pack every night. Referred by his doctor after abnormal liver tests. Thinks the doctor is overreacting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm Dan. Grab a seat wherever — fair warning, the chair by the window wobbles a little, so don't say I didn't warn you. So. My understanding is HR sent you over. Guessing this wasn't exactly how you planned to spend your Thursday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. It wasn't. Look, I don't even know what I'm doing here. Some guy on my crew decides to run his mouth and now I gotta sit in a... a therapy office. No offense.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: None taken, happens all the time. So tell me — from your side, what actually went down out there?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What went down is a whole lot of nothing. I showed up for my shift, same as always, did my job. There was — look, I was a little tired, okay, I maybe snapped at a guy on the crew. That's it. That's the big incident. Kid's probably never worked a real job in his life and he goes crying to the foreman. Twenty years I been in construction, twenty years, never had a single write-up. One bad morning and suddenly I'm the problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you've put in two decades of solid work, and this one thing — this one morning — is being treated like some kind of major incident, when from where you're sitting, it really wasn't.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Exactly. I'm not some liability, alright? I run a tight site. I know what I'm doing. And now they got me sitting here like I'm... like I got a problem or something. I don't have a problem. I come home, I have a few beers, I decompress — every guy on my crew does the same thing. That's just how it works.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Running a construction crew for twenty years, managing a site — that's genuinely not nothing. That takes a lot out of a person. You clearly take real pride in your work.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I do. I do take pride in it. That's what pisses me off about all this. I've never given them a reason — I mean, yeah, okay, I've had some rough mornings lately, but... everybody does. It's a stressful job. You try framing in August heat sometime.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Rough mornings lately — I want to make sure I'm hearing that right. And I also know your doctor flagged something recently. Liver enzymes, I think? What's your read on all that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My doctor's... I mean, yeah, he said something about my, uh, my liver enzymes being elevated or whatever. I don't — I didn't really... he made it sound like a bigger deal than it probably is. Doctors always do that. But I've been more tired lately. And I had this weird thing with my stomach for a few weeks, but... look, I'm 42, okay? That stuff happens.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you've got HR on one side, your doctor on the other, and meanwhile your own body's been sending you some signals you've been... not totally sure what to make of. That's a lot of stuff hitting at once.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I guess. I mean... I don't know. I didn't think about it like that. It's been — it's been a lot, honestly. My wife's been on me too, which I don't really want to get into. I just... I drink because it helps me sleep, helps me wind down. I'm not stumbling around, I'm not — I'm functional. I go to work.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Work, your health, your wife — it sounds like there are things that really matter to you here. A lot riding on you being okay. What would it mean for you if the drinking actually is connected to some of this — the liver thing, the rough mornings?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... huh. I don't know. I haven't really sat with that. I guess... if the doctor's right and my liver is actually getting messed up because of it... that's not great. I got a kid starting college next year. I can't be — I can't be out of commission. I need to be working.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, because there's actually quite a bit here. You've spent twenty years building something — your reputation, your career, your ability to provide for your family. And right now you've got your job flagging you, your doctor flagging you, your wife's worried, and your own body's been telling you something's off. You walked in here pretty clear that there's no problem. I'm not here to tell you there is or there isn't — that's yours to figure out. But it sounds like part of you is starting to wonder if maybe it's worth taking a closer look.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

Yeah. Maybe. I'm not — I'm not ready to call it a problem. But... yeah. Maybe it's worth figuring out what's actually going on.

client_context: A 38-year-old mandated by court to attend counseling after a second DUI. Furious about being forced to be here. Sees the system as unfair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again, Marcus. So — check in with me. How's the past couple weeks been?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: How's it been? Are you serious right now? It's been garbage. I'm still stuck driving across town every week when I got actual things to do with my time. Nothing's changed. Nothing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Still feels like this whole thing is just... an imposition. Like your time is being taken from you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's exactly what it is. You know what I missed last week? My kid's soccer game. Had to drive out here for that group session instead. For what? So some counselor can tell me I'm an alcoholic? I had two beers. Two.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about that — missing his game.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What do you want me to say? It pissed me off. He asked me afterward if I was there and I had to... I had to tell him no. And yeah, okay, that sucked. But that's on the court, not on me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That really stung. Having to say no to him.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Don't — don't try to flip this into some big therapy moment about my kid, alright? I'm here because I have to be here. I blew a point-oh-nine. Barely over the limit. My buddy Donnie drives around hammered every weekend, nothing ever happens to him. The whole system is a damn joke and I'm the one doing the hoops.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It landed on you and not him, and that feels completely arbitrary.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. And now I've got my manager at work starting to ask questions about why I'm leaving early on Thursdays. I haven't told anyone. If they find out about the DUI — I drive a company vehicle sometimes. I work in logistics. I could actually lose my job over this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's real pressure building at work that you're carrying on top of everything else. What does it feel like sitting with that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't... I mean, I didn't even think about it at first. I figured I'd show up, do my time, and that'd be it. But now it's been two months and the job thing is new and I'm just... I don't know. It's starting to feel like a lot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's an honest thing to say. A lot of guys who come through here spend months telling me everything's fine.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I have been saying that. Telling myself it's fine. But then last Thursday in group there's this guy, been sober four years, and he's talking about what drinking cost him — his kids, his job — and I just kept thinking... I don't want to be sitting there saying that stuff in four years. I still got those things.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something shifted listening to him.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe. I mean — yeah. I'm not saying I'm like him. I don't think I am. But the stuff about his kids... I've still got my son. I'm still holding onto all of it. Barely, but. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in today with a full tank of anger — still feeling the unfairness of all this, missing the game, the job pressure. And at the same time, something that guy said in group actually got to you. Both of those things are sitting in the same room right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I guess that's about right. When you say it like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you want things to look like a year from now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want any of this. I don't want to be hiding stuff from my boss, sneaking out early, lying. I don't want to be missing my kid's games. I just want things to be... normal. Like before all this started.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've got a pretty clear picture of what you're protecting. What would be one small thing — something realistic — that would feel like a step toward that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know... maybe just stop pretending everything's fine all the time? Like, even to myself. I've been — um — I've been telling myself this whole thing is a joke so I don't have to think about why I'm actually here. That's... yeah. That's probably not helping.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That kind of honesty — with yourself — that's actually harder than anything I could ask you to do in here. And you just did it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...I haven't had anything to drink in six weeks. I didn't even — I wasn't going to bring that up. I just don't want people looking at me like I'm broken. I'm not broken. I just... made some bad calls.

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's good to see you, Harold. I know it's been a... a hard few days. When you're ready, I'd love to hear from you — how are you doing right now, in this moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm... I don't know. Embarrassed, I guess. I didn't think it would come to the ER. I really didn't. I keep telling myself it wasn't that serious but then, you know, they kept me overnight and... I don't know what to make of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something about that night scared you. Even if part of you is still saying it wasn't a big deal... another part of you is sitting here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's fair. I mean, I'd been drinking more than usual that week. More than I should've. My daughter called and I just — I didn't want to talk to her. So I had a few more. And then a few more after that. And I woke up on the kitchen floor and I couldn't... I couldn't quite get up right away.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You were alone on that floor. ...... That image — that stays with me, Harold. I wonder if it stays with you too.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It does. More than I want to admit. You know, when I retired — I thought it was gonna be, like, freedom. Fish, travel, all of it. But then Margaret passed, what, three years ago now, and the days just got... long. Real long. The house is quiet. It's so quiet. And I started having a drink in the afternoon just to... I don't know. Fill it up a little, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That quiet... it sounds like it carries a lot of grief in it. What do you miss most, when you think about who you were before all of this — before the quiet took over?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Feeling like I mattered somewhere. I was an engineer for thirty-two years. People needed what I knew. And then one day you're just... not. You're just some old man in a house. My kids are busy, which is fine, that's how it should be, but... I used to know what I was for. Now I don't. And the drinking — I think it was the only time I stopped feeling that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What I'm hearing is — the drinking wasn't really about the alcohol. It was about finding some relief from a pain that's been there since Margaret died, since you stopped feeling like yourself. That's not weakness, Harold. That's a man trying to survive something enormous.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never thought about it like that. I just thought I was... being stupid. Weak, like you said. But yeah. Yeah, I think that's right. It worked, for a little while. Until it really, really didn't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Until it really didn't. ...... So if the drinking was trying to solve something — trying to fill that quiet, get some relief from the grief — what would it mean to you to find something else? Something that actually worked?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It would mean... I'd have to actually face all of it, I guess. The loneliness. The — losing Margaret. Getting old. I've been running from that for a long time. But I'm tired of running. I'm sixty-five years old and I'm tired, and I woke up on my kitchen floor, and... I don't want that to be the story. I don't want that to be how it ends.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't want that to be the story. ...... Tell me — what do you want the story to be?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to see my grandkids grow up. I want to call my daughter back when she calls, instead of pouring a drink. I'd like to, I don't know, maybe find something to do with myself that means something again. I built things my whole life. Maybe I can still do that somehow. In some way. I think I want to try.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Harold, I want to hold that for a moment. You came in here today — after one of the hardest nights of your life — and you didn't hide. You talked about Margaret, about the quiet, about waking up on that floor and deciding that isn't the ending you want. You said you want to be there for your grandkids. You said you want to build something again. That man who walked in here today — he already knows what he's reaching for. I'd like to keep meeting with him, if you're willing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I'm willing. I actually... I actually feel a little lighter saying it out loud. First time in a while. I'll be back.

client_context: A 39-year-old diagnosed with depression who self-medicates with alcohol. Has tried therapy before and dropped out. Skeptical but willing to give it one more try.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for making it in. I know you're between classes and I know you just came from the ER, so I don't want to waste your time. Can you tell me a little about what brought you in last night?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Look, I... they kind of pushed me to come here. The discharge nurse or whoever. I'm not like some guy who can't hold it together - I work, I show up to things, I'm not sleeping on a bench somewhere. It was just a bad night. I mixed some stuff I shouldn't have and it got... out of hand. That's it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the way you see it - this isn't who you are. You're a functioning person who had one bad night, and you don't want to be put in a box because of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Yeah. I... [exhales] Look, I've done therapy before. Dropped out after like six sessions. It wasn't... I don't know, it just didn't go anywhere. So I'm not exactly jumping up and down to be here. No offense.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: None taken. What was missing the last time - what made you walk away?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It felt like we were just... circling around stuff. Childhood, my dad, all that. And I'm sitting there thinking, okay but I'm depressed right now and I drink too much right now and that's the actual problem. I know the two are connected. I'm not an idiot. I just - I don't know how to stop the loop. That's what scares me, I guess. That maybe I can't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You named that yourself - the loop, the connection between the depression and the drinking. A lot of people I talk to take months to get there. And you showed up here the morning after an ER visit. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... [pause] maybe. I don't know if knowing it does anything though. Like, I know exactly what I'm doing when I pour drink number three at midnight. I know it. And I do it anyway because the other option is just sitting there feeling like... nothing. Empty. And that's worse. At least the drinking is something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull this together and you tell me if I'm off. You're not here because someone proved you have a problem - you're here because some part of you is exhausted. Exhausted by the loop: feel bad, drink, feel worse, repeat. You've tried to get out of it before, it didn't work, so you're skeptical this will either. And underneath all of that is this... quiet fear that maybe the loop is just permanent.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...yeah. That's pretty much it. [long pause] I'm 39. I thought I'd have more figured out by now. I've got a decent job, I'm in this program, and I still come home and it's like... what's the point. And I hate that I think that. I hate it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you imagine having more figured out - not perfectly, just better - what does that actually look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Just... waking up and not immediately dreading the day. Going to bed without needing something to shut my brain off first. That sounds so basic but I can't remember the last time that happened. [quiet, humorless laugh] I used to be able to do that. So yeah, I don't know, maybe that's still in there somewhere.

client_context: A 26-year-old software engineer with severe social anxiety who uses alcohol as liquid courage at every social event. Knows it's a crutch but terrified of life without it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in. I know referrals like this can feel a little out of nowhere — like, 'wait, what did I say?' So before we get into anything, I just want to hear from you directly: what's your sense of why you're here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I'm not totally sure. Dr. Patel asked me a bunch of questions at my physical — like the standard screening stuff — and I just answered honestly and then she said she wanted me to talk to someone. So. Here I am. I don't really think it's a big deal, I just drink at social things like everyone else my age does.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you were straightforward with her, answered everything honestly, and here you are — even though your own read on things is that it's not really a problem.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, I work in tech — do you know what happy hours are like? It's basically mandatory. I'm not drinking alone in my apartment or anything. It's just... social stuff. I drink when there are people around.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Social situations — tell me more about what those are like for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: They're... I mean, I have really bad anxiety. Like, diagnosed, on medication, the whole thing. Being in groups of people is just — it's a lot. I know it probably sounds ridiculous for someone my age but I genuinely cannot walk into a party and just be normal without having a couple drinks first. Otherwise I'm standing in a corner counting ceiling tiles and convincing myself everyone thinks I'm weird.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So alcohol gives you access to a version of yourself that can actually be in the room. Without it, you're kind of... locked out.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's — yeah, that's actually exactly it. And I've tried just going to things sober and it's awful. My heart races, I can't think of anything to say, I stand there convinced I'm coming across as this total weirdo. At least with a drink or two I can laugh and have actual conversations and feel like... a person. Like I belong there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to reflect something back to you, because I think it matters. You've actually tested this — you've shown up sober, noticed what happened, and formed a real opinion about it. That's not someone who hasn't thought about this. That's someone paying close attention to their own life.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess I have thought about it more than I usually admit. It's just... I don't know how to be social without it. Like that skill never really developed in me. And I'm 26, not 16 — I feel like I should have figured this out by now. My friends don't need three drinks to introduce themselves to a stranger at a networking thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just check I'm understanding you right. You've got real anxiety — not just shyness — and alcohol has been the bridge that lets you get through social situations. You've tried without it and it was genuinely hard. And at the same time, there's a part of you that's been tracking this, maybe wondering if this is how it's supposed to work long-term. Does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's it. And honestly the reason I answered Dr. Patel's questions honestly instead of just... fudging them... was because I'm kind of tired? Like I'm tired of my whole social life being this logistical puzzle — how much can I drink, who's driving, is there going to be alcohol there, how do I pace myself. It takes up so much mental space. It's exhausting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a significant thing to say — that you're tired of organizing your life around it. I'm curious: when you imagine things being different, what does that actually look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think about it sometimes. Like... my best friend's getting married next year and I want to actually be present for that. Not just loosened up enough to function. And I've read some stuff about exposure therapy for social anxiety — like actually treating the underlying thing instead of just... managing around it. I don't know if that's realistic for me specifically, but it's something I've thought about.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The fact that you walked in here, answered honestly, and you're already thinking about treating what's underneath this — that's not a small thing. A lot of people spend years not getting to that question. And you've named something really clear: you want to be present in your life, not just functional in it. That's something worth building toward.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I think... I think I'm ready to at least try something different. I don't know exactly what that looks like yet but — I don't want to be 35 and still needing a drink to make a phone call, you know? That's not the person I want to be.

client_context: A 55-year-old who lost their spouse 8 months ago and has been drinking to numb the pain. Isolated from friends and family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, good to see you — I was a little worried when you rescheduled twice. Not gonna lie, I had a whole dramatic rescue scenario planned. How've you been since we last met?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Ha. Well, no rescue needed. I'm fine. I mean... not fine, I guess. It's been a week. Or two weeks. They all kind of blend together lately, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The days blending together — that sounds like it's gotten heavier since we last talked. What happened?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... look, I slipped up, okay? A few times. But I'm not back to where I was, I want to be clear about that. It's just — my daughter called and she wants to sell the house. Richard's house. And I had a couple glasses of wine. More than a couple. But it wasn't... it's not a big deal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a lot to land on you — the house, your daughter, all of it at once. What's going on inside when you think about letting it go?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He built that porch. With his own hands, you know? Took him three summers. And she just... she doesn't get it. Nobody gets it. I was sitting out there looking at it and I just — I needed something. I don't even know what I needed. I just needed something to make it quiet.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You needed something to make it quiet. And the wine was there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. And I know — I know I'm supposed to call someone when that happens. I have your number. I have my friend Carol's number. But it was eleven o'clock at night and I just... I felt stupid. Like I should be able to handle this by now. It's been eight months. People move on.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Eight months is not a deadline, and you know that. But what I'm actually noticing is — you didn't call Carol at eleven because you didn't want to be a burden to her. That's not weakness. That's you caring about someone else even when you're in pain. That's actually kind of remarkable.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... huh. I never thought about it like that. I just thought I was being pathetic. Carol keeps saying call anytime, and maybe I could've. I just don't want to be — I don't want to be the sad widow everyone feels sorry for. I used to be the one people called.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You used to be the one people leaned on. And somewhere in the last eight months that flipped, and it doesn't sit right with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. No, it doesn't. I want to be... I want to be myself again. I don't know if that's even possible without Richard, but... I want to try. I think I do. I actually — yeah. I want to try.

client_context: A 27-year-old bartender who drinks after every shift. Recently realized they can't remember the last sober day. Starting to question if this is normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again. So... how have things been since we last spoke?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... not great, honestly. Had a pretty bad week. I know we talked about cutting back and I was doing alright for a little while, but then I don't know, everything just kind of fell apart again. And now I'm back here and I'm just... I'm pissed, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You had some real momentum going, and then it slipped — and that's frustrating.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. And it's like... I didn't even make a decision to drink more, it just happened. My coworker called in sick, I was covering doubles all week, long nights. And the drinks are just — they're literally right in front of me all night. What am I supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really tough environment to be trying to navigate any of this in. What was it like during the stretch when things were going better?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I was... counting. Actually counting drinks. Keeping it to like two or three after a shift instead of just drinking until close. Which I know that's still drinking, but it felt different. Like I had some — I don't know. Control, I guess. It felt weird to say that out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something shifted — you were in charge of it, instead of it being in charge of you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Kind of, yeah. But then this week happened and I'm like... what was the point? I can't change the fact that I'm a bartender. That's my job. I'm not gonna quit.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And I'd never ask you to walk away from something that's yours. What I want to say is — you came back here after a hard week. You showed up anyway. That matters.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I have to. Court says so. [pause] ...But okay. Yeah. I did want to talk about it. I didn't want to just not show up and pretend everything was fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you wanted to be here. To be honest. [pause] Can I ask — when you said last time that you couldn't remember the last sober day, what goes through your mind when that thought comes up?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It... freaks me out, honestly. Like I said it kind of offhand last session but then I went home and I was actually trying to think back and I couldn't — I couldn't find one. Not in months. Maybe longer. And that kind of messed with me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That realization stayed with you. Even through this rough week, it's been sitting there in the background.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And I don't want to make it into a bigger deal than it is, but... I also don't know. Like my dad drinks. My uncle drinks. All the guys at the bar drink. So where's the line, you know? Where does it go from just... life, to like, an actual problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's such an important question to be sitting with. And I wonder — what does your gut say?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That it's... [long pause] ...I don't know if it's normal. Like, normal people don't count. My coworker just has one beer and he's done, he doesn't even think about it. I think about it during my shift. I'm already thinking about what I'm gonna have after while I'm still working. And that's... that's probably not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really honest thing to say. It takes something to look at yourself that clearly.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't feel like it's courageous or whatever. I feel kind of scared, actually.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That fear makes a lot of sense. And I'm curious — underneath it, is there any part of you that can imagine what a different life might look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, actually. I mean I don't know exactly what it would look like but... I'd probably sleep better. And I've been wanting to get back to lifting — I used to work out a lot in college and I just stopped because I'm always too tired or too hungover on my days off. Which is kind of dumb when I say it out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just take a moment to reflect back what I'm hearing. You came in today frustrated and honest about a hard week — and that took something. And underneath all of it, there's a part of you that's already picturing a different version of your life. Better sleep, getting back to things that used to matter to you. The drinking is starting to feel less like just 'how things are' and more like something that's getting in the way.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it like that... yeah. It has been getting in the way for a while. I just didn't want to admit that to myself because then I'd actually have to do something about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And now you're here — and maybe you're starting to feel ready to think about what 'doing something' might look like. On your terms, at your pace.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe. I mean... yeah. I think so. I don't know what it looks like yet but I'm not as — I don't know, I'm not as closed off about it as I was even a month ago. Like even being here, I used to hate coming. Today it feels different. I actually want to figure this out.

client_context: A 40-year-old single parent who has been drinking a bottle of wine nightly to cope with the stress of raising two kids alone. Knows it's too much but feels trapped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. I'm Sarah, one of the counselors here. I know this wasn't exactly your choice to be here today, and I appreciate you showing up anyway. Before we get into anything, is there anything you need — water, anything — to get comfortable?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm fine. Look, I don't — I'm only here because the court said I had to be. So. I'm here. That's what I can give you.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Court-ordered, not your idea. What's that been like — going through all of this over the past few weeks?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What do you think it's been like? It's been humiliating. I'm a forty-year-old woman with two kids and I have to come sit in a — a clinic — and talk to a stranger because I had some drinks. My neighbors saw the police car. My kids were home. It's been a complete nightmare.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So on top of everything else, it became very public, very fast. And you're sitting here feeling like you're being treated as if you have some serious problem — when from where you're standing, that's not really the full picture of who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. I made one mistake. One. And suddenly I'm being treated like I'm some kind of... I don't know, like I'm some addict or something. I am not an addict. I am a mother who is just trying to keep herself together.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Keeping it together — I want to understand what that actually looks like. What does a regular day in your life look like right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... I mean, it's a lot. I work full time, I pick up the kids, I make dinner, help with homework, get them to bed. By the time they're asleep I'm just... done. Completely done. And I sit down and I pour myself a glass of wine to unwind. That's not a crime. That's just surviving.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So by the time the house is quiet, you've been running on empty since morning — and that wine is really the only moment in the whole day that belongs just to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. And... I mean, okay, I know it's become more than a glass. I'm not stupid. But that doesn't make me an addict. That makes me exhausted. There's a difference.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just said something really honest — that it's become more than a glass. I don't want to skip past that, because that took something to say out loud. When you say more than a glass, what does that actually look like on a typical night?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: A bottle. Most nights. I know how that sounds.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You know how it sounds, and you said it anyway. There's something real in that — you can see this clearly even if you're not sure yet what to do with what you're seeing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've... yeah. I've thought about it, I'm not oblivious. I just — I don't have another way right now. My mom used to help with the kids and she passed last year, and their dad is completely out of the picture, so it's just me. There's no one else. There's literally no backup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Losing your mom and doing all of this completely alone at the same time — that's an enormous amount to carry. When you do let yourself sit with the worry about the drinking, what scares you most?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My kids. That's... that's the thing. My older one is thirteen and she's sharp. She doesn't say anything but I catch her looking at me sometimes when I go for a second glass. And I hate that I notice that look and then pour it anyway. I hate that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I've heard, make sure I've got it right. You're carrying everything alone — full-time work, two kids, grieving your mom. The wine is the one thing at the end of the day that gives you any relief, and it's grown to a bottle most nights. You don't see yourself as having a problem, and at the same time part of you does see it. And the thing that worries you most is your daughter, and what she's starting to notice. Does that feel accurate?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's pretty much it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So if nothing changed — a year from now, two years from now — where do you see things going?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't... I don't really want to think about that. Honestly I think it gets worse. I think I end up in a situation way worse than this. Lose my job maybe. My daughter pulls away from me. I don't know. That's not — that's not what I want for them.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You can see a version of the future you don't want, and you named it. A lot of people can't do that — or won't. The fact that you can means something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... I don't want to be the mom who drinks herself to sleep every night. That's not who I am. I didn't — this isn't what I planned. I didn't plan for any of this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You know who you are, and you know who you want to be for those kids. So I want to ask — is there any part of you that would want to look at what some support might look like? Even just small steps, nothing overwhelming.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... yeah. Maybe. I don't even know what that would look like, honestly, I've never done anything like this before. But yeah. I guess that's why I'm here. I didn't think I'd say that walking in, but... yeah.

client_context: A 16-year-old whose parents found empty bottles hidden in their room. Brought to counseling against their will. Scared but trying to act tough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, you actually showed up. I'll be honest — I had a small bet with myself about whether I'd see you today. Glad I lost.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My mom drove me. It's not like I had a choice.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Right, so you're here because you had to be. I get that. What's going through your head right now, sitting in that chair again?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Nothing. I just want this to be over. Can we like... do whatever and then I can go home?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Last time you mentioned the lab results kind of caught you off guard. I've been thinking about that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: They were probably wrong. Doctors mess stuff up all the time. My cousin — they thought he had diabetes and he was totally fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Could be. Either way — do you remember what the results actually said?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... elevated liver enzymes or whatever. Which like — that happens for a ton of reasons. It's not automatically serious.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're right, it does happen for a lot of reasons. And you've clearly done some thinking about it since we last talked.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I Googled it. There's like, fast food, medications, whatever. It doesn't mean anything specific.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What else came up when you were looking into it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know, like regular stuff. Alcohol was on the list but it's on every list. I barely even drink so it's not — that's not what this is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Barely drink. I want to make sure I'm hearing you right — what does barely mean to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like... a few times a week, maybe. Sometimes more on weekends. But it's not every single day, so it's not like I'm an alcoholic or something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A few times a week, and you're sixteen. Not trying to pile on — but that's actually more than most adults drink. I noticed you kind of paused when you said the number out loud.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... yeah. I mean. When you say it like that it sounds... I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's going through your head right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's just... it started as like, something to do when I was bored. My friends were doing it. And now I'm sitting here talking to some therapist about my liver and... that's a weird thing to be happening to me. Like that's not supposed to be my life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Sixteen, started out just killing time, and now here we are talking about lab results. And some part of you is sitting with the fact that this isn't where you thought you'd be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want it to be like... a thing. You know? An actual thing. I don't want to be the kid with a problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not ready to be defined by this. That makes complete sense. And I'll say — the fact that you came back today, even pissed off about it, even because your mom drove you — that's not nothing. That tells me something about what you actually want for yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to play varsity soccer next year. My coach said if I keep my grades up and stay out of trouble... like that's actually something I care about. And I haven't even been going to practice as much lately because I'm tired all the time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Soccer. That's real. So what would it look like — and I'm genuinely asking, not trying to back you into a corner — what would it look like to still hang out with your friends on weekends and also actually make that happen?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... probably cutting back at least. Maybe a lot. I don't know, like, the drinking isn't even that fun anymore, I'm just doing it because it's there. I could find other stuff to do. Probably.
